# Meshes and solids ## What to do - A `` holds one shape and one material (`raea/mesh`). Sizes are scene units (think metres: a phone is 0.15, a person 1.8, a room 4). The shapes, Bevy's primitives with Bevy's fields, all centred on the Mesh3d's translation: - `` (half sizes, as Bevy's) - `` - ``, standing along y - ``, point up - ``, lying in the x-y plane (turn the Mesh3d by `Math.PI / 2` about x to lay it flat) - ``, standing along y - ``: `normal={[0, 0, 1]}` faces +z (a wall), `[0, 1, 0]` up (a floor, Bevy's default) - `Text3D size depth`: solid letters, centred, e.g. `SALE` - Place and turn a Mesh3d with its transform: `Transform.fromXyz(x, y, z)`, `.withRotation(Quat.fromEuler("XYZ", rx, ry, rz))` (radians), `.withScale([x, y, z])`. All three may change every frame (a pillar growing, a squash on landing). - Model anything else as a Manifold solid and pass it as ``: `manifold.box(w, h, d)`, `roundedBox(w, h, d, r)`, `sphere(r)`, `cylinder(r, h)` (along z), `cone(r1, r2, h)` (a tapered cylinder too), `torus(R, r)` and `text3d(text, size, depth)`, combined with `.union()`, `.minus()`, `.intersect()`, `.hull()`, moved with `.move(x, y, z)`, `.rotate(x, y, z)` (**degrees**) and `.scale(...)`. Build a solid once at module level, never per frame, and move the Mesh3d instead. - Give a Mesh3d a `name` when it comes and goes, or swaps places with another of the same shape. ## Many copies: ``, `scatter()` and `` (`raea/3d`) - `` draws one glTF at every placement, loaded once and drawn by the GPU as instances; without `src`, a geometry child (or `shape={solid}`) and a material child draw a mesh at every placement. Each placement is `{ position, rotation?, scale? }` (radians). A list that changes moves the copies (each distinct list is kept, so thousands moving every frame cost a list a frame); moving, turning, scaling or hiding the whole set with the Instances' own props costs nothing. The count is the first frame's. Copies share one surface and play no clip. `shadow={false}` for grass and flowers by the thousand. - `scatter({ area: { min: [x0, z0], max: [x1, z1] }, count, spacing, avoid, margin, clearOf, seed, yaw, tilt, scale, y, density })` makes the placements: seeded (the same every frame, render and play), at least `spacing` apart, off the `avoid` boxes, on the ground height `y(x, z)`, kept where `density(x, z)` says. Call it once at module level. - `` is a lawn or a meadow the engine grows itself from functions of the ground, cut into tiles with detail by distance; under `` the wind bends it. ## Organic shapes and growth: `sdf` and `grow` (`raea/3d`) - **Blended bodies.** A creature, a limb, a handle grown out of a body, or a melted form is a distance field. Build it from `sdf.sphere`, `box`, `capsule(a, b, r)`, `cone(a, b, ra, rb)`, `tube([[x, y, z, r], ...])`, `ellipsoid`, `torus` and `cylinder` (y up, metres). - Join the parts with `sdf.smoothUnion(k, ...)`. Within `k` metres of each join it blends them into one surface, which is what makes the parts read as one thing. - Carve with `smoothSubtract(k, a, b)`, for example an eye socket. - Modify with `.move`, `.rotate` (degrees), `.scale`, `.mirrorX()` (both sides from one), `.round(r)`, `.shell(t)` and `.displace(amp, freq, octaves, seed)` (bark, rock, lumpy skin). - `.solid(step)` meshes the field into a Solid. The default cell is a 96th of its size; pass about a third of the thinnest part. Cut, union and measure it like any solid. - **Grown things.** These are seeded, so the same settings give the same shape on every frame: - `grow.tree({ height, crown: "dome"|"sphere"|"cone"|"column"|"umbrella"|"vase", points, leaves, seed }, "wood"|"leaves")` grows branches into the crown's shape by space colonization, thinned from trunk to twig. Draw the wood and the leaves as two meshes with two materials. With `points` 600-2000 a tree is 20k-120k triangles: put a forest in ``. - `grow.loft([[0, "circle 0.2"], [0.3, "circle 0.3"], [0.6, "rect 0.1 0.1"]])` skins outlines at heights into a vase, a bottle, a lamp base or a column. An outline is `circle r`, `ellipse rx rz`, `rect w d`, `ngon n r`, or `[x, z]` points. - `grow.terrain({ size, height, freq, seed, flat })` is ground as a closed slab. `flat` clears a disc in the middle to stand things on, and the slab can be cut with `minus` for a path or a pond. - `grow.boulder({ size, squash, rough, seed })` is a rock resting on y 0. - `grow.rosette({ leaves, length, tilt, rise })` is a succulent, an agave, a lettuce or a flower's petals, set at the golden angle and blended from one heart. ## Lines and curves: `Line3d` and `Tube` (`raea/mesh`) A line through points, such as a graph's curve, a route on a map, a drawn stroke or a wire, is one part: `` (flat, a `width`, round at its joins and ends) or `` (round, a `radius`). Give it the points in order and its material as its child. `p` is how much of it is drawn, 0 to 1 of its length, so animating `p` draws the line on, and it stays one part, solid at every frame. ```tsx const pts = Array.from({ length: 64 }, (_, i) => [i / 16 - 2, Math.sin(i / 6) * 0.5, 0] as [number, number, number]); const p = interpolate(frame, [0, 40], [0, 1], { extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp" }); ``` - Give enough points for the curve to read smooth (a point every few degrees of turn); the line is straight between them. - A Line3d lies in its points' plane and faces along that plane's normal; for a line seen edge-on, give `normal`, or use a Tube. - Never build a curve from a chain of boxes, one a segment (`NAME-0`, `NAME-1`, ...). A part mounts on the frame it first appears, so a growing chain comes in a chunk at a time and its joins show. ## Text in the 3D world, animated glyph by glyph (`RichText`) `` is flat lettering standing in the scene: every glyph its own lit, shaded entity (it takes the lights, casts a letter-shaped shadow, and things in front hide it). Use it for titles, signs and captions that animate in; use `Text3D` for solid, extruded letters. - Props: `size` (the em in metres, 0.5), `font`, `weight`, `italic`, `color`, `align` (left/center/right edge at `position`), `lineHeight`, `maxWidth` (wraps), `roughness`, `metalness`, `emissive`, `emissiveIntensity`, `unlit`, `castShadow`, `name` (its glyphs are then `name:0`, `name:1`... for world.*). - Runs: `Hello world`. - Per glyph, with 2D's moves: `enter="pop"` (or `["pop", "rise"]`, `slide({ from: "left" })`...) `each={3}` frames apart from `at`, `by="word"` to stagger words; `exit` + `exitAt` (+ `exitEach`). Move px count 100 to the em. - A typewriter: `reveal={(frame - 10) / 2}` (glyphs shown; the next fades in over the fraction). - Free motion: `glyph={(g) => ({ position, rotation, scale, color, opacity, visible })}`, `g` = { index, count, char, word, words, inWord, wordLength, line, span }; compute from `useCurrentFrame()`, `spring`, `interpolate` as in 2D. - The text itself is fixed for the part's life (like a mesh's shape); change it by giving another `name`. ## Manifold in full (`raea/3d`) Everything below returns a new Solid (or CrossSection) and leaves the old one as it was. Build at module level. - **Solids from scratch**: `manifold.box`, `roundedBox`, `sphere`, `cylinder` (along z), `cone(r1, r2, h)`, `torus`, `text3d`; `manifold.extrude(outline, h, {divisions, twist, scaleTop})` and `manifold.revolve(outline, {degrees, segments})` from a 2D shape; `manifold.levelSet(sdf, {min, max, resolution})` from a signed distance function (negative inside); `manifold.hull([[x, y, z], ...])` from points; `manifold.fromMesh(verts, tris)` and `manifold.import("x.glb")` from triangles. - **Booleans**: `a.union(b, c)`, `a.minus(b)`, `a.intersect(b)`; for many at once `manifold.union(...list)`, `manifold.difference(first, ...cutters)`, `manifold.intersection(...list)`; `manifold.compose(...)` holds solids that don't touch as one, `s.decompose()` splits a solid into its separate pieces. - **Moves**: `.move(x, y, z)`, `.rotate(x, y, z)` (degrees), `.scale(s)` or `.scale(x, y, z)`, `.mirror(nx, ny, nz)`, `.transform([12 numbers, column by column])`, `.warp((x, y, z) => [x, y + x * x, z])` (refine first so there are vertices to bend: `.refineToLength(0.05).warp(...)`). - **Cutting**: `.trim(nx, ny, nz, offset)` keeps the normal's side of a plane; `.splitByPlane(...)` gives both halves; `.split(cutter)` gives [inside, outside]. - **Surfaces**: `.refine(n)`, `.refineToLength(len)`, `.refineToTolerance(tol)`, `.smooth({angle, refine})` (a box becomes a pebble), `.simplify(tol)`; `.hull(...others)` wraps them; `.minkowski(manifold.sphere(0.05))` rounds every edge, `.minkowskiDiff(...)` erodes. - **2D shapes** (`crossSection`): `crossSection.rect(w, h)`, `circle(r)`, `polygon(points)`, `hull(points)`, `of(contours)`; then `.union/.minus/.intersect`, `.offset(d, {join: "round" | "miter" | "square" | "bevel"})` (grow or, negative, shrink), `.hull()`, `.minkowski()`, `.move(x, y)`, `.rotate(deg)`, `.scale()`, `.mirror()`, `.simplify()`, `.decompose()`, and `.extrude(h, ...)` / `.revolve(...)` into a solid. `outline.rect/circle/polygon` are the same shapes as plain arrays. - **From 3D back to 2D**: `s.project()` is its shadow on the x-y plane (seen down the z axis, so project before standing a solid up), `s.crossSection(z)` its slice at height z, both CrossSections to offset and extrude again (a base plate that follows a model's footprint). - **Asking**: `.volume()`, `.area()`, `.genus()` (holes through it), `.bounds()`, `.triangles()`, `.isEmpty()`, `.slice(z)` ({area, contours, polygons}), `.minGap(other, searchLength)`, `.rayCast(from, to)` (where a line meets the surface: put one thing on top of another), `.export("x.glb")`. Extruded and revolved shapes grow along z: `.rotate(-90, 0, 0)` stands them up along y, the scene's up. ```tsx // a vase: a profile revolved (along z) and hollowed, a base from its footprint (project looks down z), then the whole // piece stood up along y const profile = crossSection.polygon([[0, 0], [0.3, 0], [0.45, 0.3], [0.25, 0.8], [0.3, 1], [0, 1]]); const outer = profile.revolve({ segments: 64 }); const body = outer.minus(outer.scale(0.88, 0.88, 1).move(0, 0, 0.06)); const base = body.project().offset(0.08).extrude(0.05).move(0, 0, -0.05); const vase = body.union(base).rotate(-90, 0, 0); ``` ## Why Every geometry reaches the engine as a Manifold expression (`box(1, 2, 3)`), built once per distinct expression and cached, then drawn by Bevy. A modelled solid and a primitive travel the same way. ## Common mistakes - Two shapes, or none, in a Mesh3d: give it exactly one, plus one material. - A shape's size that changes per frame (a cuboid growing by its `half_size`): that's a new shape each frame. Animate the transform's scale. - Degrees in `Quat.fromEuler`, radians in `.rotate()`: it's the other way round. - `half_size` given full sizes: the cuboid comes out twice as big. Bevy's sizes are halves. - A Plane3d facing +z as a floor: it stands up like a wall. Give it `normal={[0, 1, 0]}`, or use a thin Cuboid. - Text3D with quotes or backslashes in it: they throw. - A 2D outline revolved with points at negative x: revolve takes x >= 0 (the axis is x = 0). - Building solids inside the component body: every frame rebuilds them. Build once (module level, `??=`). - A curve drawn as a chain of parts (a box a segment): it grows in chunks with its joins showing. Use one `Line3d` or `Tube` and animate its `p`. ## Example: a sign with the word cut through it, and solid letters in front ```tsx import { AbsoluteFill, Composition, registerRoot, useCurrentFrame } from "raea"; import { Cone, Text3D, manifold, type Solid } from "raea/3d"; import { StandardMaterial } from "raea/pbr"; import { Mesh3d } from "raea/mesh"; import { AmbientLight, DirectionalLight } from "raea/light"; import { Quat, Transform } from "raea/transform"; import { Camera3d } from "raea/camera"; let sign: Solid | null = null; const getSign = () => (sign ??= manifold.roundedBox(2.6, 1.1, 0.25, 0.1).minus(manifold.text3d("OPEN", 0.6, 0.6))); function Sign() { const f = useCurrentFrame(); return ( DAILY ); } registerRoot(() => ); ```

# Bevy plugins from TypeScript: declare, build, generate, call

Any Bevy plugin (crates.io, git or a local path) joins raea without hand-written Rust, unless it needs a protocol or a
predicted simulation. The design and results are in `sdk/raea/docs/bevy-plugins.md`.

**A plugin in the catalog needs no declaration of your own.** The catalog (`sdk/raea/bench/bevy-plugins/package.json`)
is generated into the SDK, so any project imports a plugin's wrappers, types and handle by its name:

```tsx
import { ColliderConstructor, RigidBody } from "raea/plugins/avian";
import { Bloom } from "raea/plugins/bevy";
import { avian, tnua } from "@raea/plugins";   // every catalog plugin's handle, by name
```

The plugin build renders and plays them (`tools/bevy-plugins.sh build sdk/raea/bench/bevy-plugins`). Declare a plugin
yourself, as below, only when the catalog doesn't have it.

## Scenario: physics with a raycast, in a scene and in a program

**1. Declare the plugin** in the project's `package.json`. Its key is the plugin's name, which is also its cargo
feature. Give one version per Bevy minor, so the 0.20 bump only reads a different line:

```json
"raea": { "plugins": {
  "avian": {
    "crate": "avian3d",
    "versions": { "0.19": "=0.7.0", "0.20": "=0.8.0" },
    "features": ["3d", "f32", "parry-f32", "collider-from-mesh"],
    "plugin": "avian3d::prelude::PhysicsPlugins::default()",
    "calls": "avian",
    "headless": ["assets", "mesh"]
  }
} }
```

(`raea.bevy.plugins`, the key's first name, is still read.) `plugin` is the expression `app.add_plugins` takes. The plugin's default features are always off, so list the ones
you need. A source can be `{"git": URL, "rev": HASH}` or `{"path": DIR}` in place of a version.

**2. Build and generate:**

```sh
tools/bevy-plugins.sh build DIR   # sync engine/bevy-plugins, build raea-bevy-sdk, regenerate when versions moved
tools/bevy-plugins.sh check DIR   # fails on drift: versions, Bevy minor, or the generated TypeScript
```

This writes `DIR/bevy/avian.gen.tsx`, generated from the built App's TypeRegistry:
- a TypeScript type for every reflected type;
- a TSX wrapper per component and resource;
- `<AvianSettings>` for the plugin's resources;
- an `avian` object of typed handles for every component, resource, event, message and state.

It also writes `DIR/bevy/plugins.lock.json`, which holds each crate's resolved version and a hash of its schema.

**3a. In a scene (render equals play)**, put the wrappers inside the Mesh3d they belong to. Mark the Mesh3d `driven`,
because the plugin owns its Transform. Keep the composition in DIR, beside `bevy/`: a baked play copies only the
composition's folder, so an import of `../bevy/` from a subfolder fails there:

```tsx
import { AvianSettings, ColliderConstructor, RigidBody } from "./bevy/avian.gen";
<AvianSettings Gravity={[0, -9.81, 0]} />
<Mesh3d name="ball" driven transform={Transform.fromXyz(0, 3, 0)}>
  <Sphere radius={0.4} /><StandardMaterial base_color="#e11d48" />
  <RigidBody value="Dynamic" />
  <ColliderConstructor value={{ Sphere: { radius: 0.4 } }} />
</Mesh3d>
```

**3b. In a program (a headless App, any plugin, any call)**, run it with `raea-bevy-sdk motion run FILE.ts`:

```ts
import { BevyApp, at, with as w } from "raea/bevy";
import { avian } from "./bevy/avian.gen";
const app = BevyApp.open({ plugins: ["avian"], fps: 60 });
const ball = app.spawn(w(avian.RigidBody, "Dynamic"), w(avian.ColliderConstructor, { Sphere: { radius: 0.5 } }), at(0, 4, 0));  // a body starts from its Transform
app.step(90);                                         // Time moves one frame per step, as in a render
app.get(ball, avian.Position);                        // typed: [number, number, number]
app.call("avian3d/cast_ray", { origin: [0, 10, 0], direction: [0, -1, 0] });   // the call bridge
```

Every App answers bevy_remote's methods:
- `world.query`, `world.get_components`, `world.insert_components`;
- `world.trigger_event`, `world.write_message` and `world.observe+watch` (`app.trigger`, `app.write`, `app.observe`);
- `registry.schema` and `schedule.list`.

It also answers raea's `raea/state.get` and `raea/state.set` (`app.state`, `app.setState`), and each plugin's
own methods. `app.methods` lists them all. `BevyApp.stepTogether([client, server], n)` steps several Apps in lockstep,
as a network's peers need.

**4. A dev tool:** `BevyApp.open({ plugins, serve: 15703 })` serves the same methods over BRP's HTTP. Use curl or
any BRP client.

## When Rust is still needed (the escape hatch)

Name a module in `engine/bevy-plugins/src/`:
- `"calls": "name"` adds methods next to a plain plugin;
- `"adapter": "name"` registers the plugin itself.

Write Rust only for:
- **non-component APIs**: SystemParam methods (`SpatialQuery::cast_ray`) and events that aren't reflected (avian's
  `CollisionStart`). Each becomes a few-line BRP method.
- **protocols and predicted simulations**: lightyear's `app.component::<T>().replicate().predict()` and the movement
  system that rollback re-runs. See `src/lightyear.rs`.
- **assets and closures**: a `Handle<EffectAsset>` or a tween's lens. Make it a reflected component of yours that
  builds the plugin's object from numbers, as hanabi's `Particles` does.
- **generic plugins**: `InputPlugin::<A>` needs a concrete type, so the adapter names it.
- **render-equals-play fixes**: a seed, a run condition on `advancing`, or WinitPlugin turned off.

A plugin that opens a window (bevy-inspector-egui, anything egui) doesn't run headless. Use the BRP server as its dev
tool instead.

## The catalog: look before declaring

`sdk/raea/bench/bevy-plugins/package.json` already declares Bevy's optional features (the builtin `bevy` entry:
gamepads, picking, every image and audio format, gizmos, dev tools, the PBR textures and LUTs, meshlets, Solari) and
about 70 ecosystem plugins: input, character controllers, tiles, asset formats, particles, cameras, UI, pathfinding,
tweening, noise, networking and dialogue. Copy an entry from there rather than writing one; each has its 0.19 and 0.20
pins, and `null` where a plugin has no release for that Bevy yet (a build on it leaves the plugin out).

Generic plugins already have adapters that TypeScript drives:
- input: `leafwing/player` and `leafwing/state` (leafwing), `enhanced_input/pawn` and `enhanced_input/state`;
- a character: `tnua/character`, then write `TnuaInput {motion, jump, crouch, dash}` each frame;
- data files: `common_assets/load` and `common_assets/get` (JSON, RON, TOML, YAML, MessagePack, CBOR, CSV);
- noise: `noise/sample`, `noise/grid`;
- schedules as Graphviz: `debugdump/schedule`.

A headless program presses keys and mouse buttons with `app.call("raea/input", { key: "Space" })` (`pressed: false`
releases). `run.sh catalog` proves each plugin alone; see "The catalog" in `sdk/raea/docs/bevy-plugins.md`.

# Post-processing: bloom, fog, light in the air, ambient occlusion, anti-aliasing, tone mapping, the lens, motion blur

## What to do

Put these beside the camera, once each:

- `<Bloom intensity threshold />`: glow around bright parts. `intensity` 1 is a natural glow, 2 strong. `threshold`
  is how bright a pixel must be to glow: 0.8-1 lets only emissive surfaces and hot highlights bloom (the usual
  choice), 0 makes everything a little dreamy. Bloom earns its place on neon, screens, sparks and lit signs; give
  those materials an `emissive` brighter than white, `LinearRgba.from(Srgba.hex(c)).mul(3)` to `.mul(10)`.
- `<Fog color near far />`: things fade into `color` between `near` and `far` (scene units from the camera), or
  `density={0.1}` for exponential haze. Use the background colour as the fog colour so distant parts dissolve into it.
- `<VolumetricFog ambient ambientColor />` with `<FogVolume>`s and `volumetric` lights: light you see in the air,
  dust in a sunbeam, smoke, a haze of blood. `<FogVolume name position scale density color absorption scattering
  anisotropy falloff />` is a box of air (`scale` is its size in metres; rotate it as a mesh). `density` 0.02 is a
  faint haze, 0.1 dust, 0.5 smoke; `color` tints what it scatters (a dark red for blood in the air); `absorption`
  darkens it like soot, `scattering` brightens it like dust; `anisotropy` near 1 makes a shaft glow when the camera
  looks toward the light; `falloff` thins it going up from the box's floor (ground fog: a wide, low box with
  `falloff={1}`). Mark the lights that should shaft through it `volumetric` (a SpotLight is the cheap one: a point
  light pays six shadow maps; a DirectionalLight works too); they cast shadows, so a wall with a window in it, a
  blind, or a bust carves the shaft.
  The fog is one medium in a grid along the view: every volume, its falloff and every `<Fire>`'s light go into the
  same cells, so overlapping volumes just mix (smoke rolling into ground fog), a volume with no density shows nothing,
  and the cost is the grid's whatever the frame's size or the number of volumes. The first two volumetric spots and
  the first two volumetric directional lights are hero lights: their shafts are integrated exactly along each
  pixel's ray over their shadow maps, so a blind's bars and a doorway's edge are as sharp as the shadow and never
  step or grain. Glass, image planes and fires (anything see-through) are fogged at their own depth. It has no
  noise to dither, so it encodes small: Mean Streets' fog shots took a third of the bitrate the march's grain did.
  Measured against a 512-step ground truth (sdk/raea/bench/bevy/fog-score.py): the rome film's curia SSIM 0.9999 at
  38 ms a frame (the march 0.9988 at 30), Mean Streets 0.979 at 11 ms (the march 0.894 at 7), the volumetric fixture
  0.966 / 52.7 dB at 7.7 ms (the march 0.751 / 28.8 dB at 3.4). `hero={false}` drops the exact shafts for the grid's
  softer ones (Mean Streets 2.8 ms a frame): use it when no shaft has a hard edge in shot. `slices` (128), `tile`
  (8 px) and `samples` (2 a cell) set the grid: more slices for a deep shot with fog close to the camera and far off.
  The rest is tuning, each prop's default the measured best: `shadow` (what dims light passing through a volume,
  "absorb"), `epipolar` (how densely the shafts are sampled), `heroExact` (every pixel integrated, the slow
  reference), `tricubic`, and under <SolariLighting> `solari` (`false`, or its candidates, history frames, sky rays,
  what lights it, filter and guide).
- `<VolumetricFog mode="march" steps dither resolution />`: Bevy's ray march through each volume instead, as raea
  drew fog before the grid. Only for matching an older piece: it grains or steps where the grid doesn't, composites
  overlapping volumes in row order, and lights a volume's whole box with `ambient`. `steps` (64) is how finely each
  ray is sampled; `dither` turns too few steps into fine grain; `resolution={0.5}` marches a quarter of the pixels.
- `<AmbientOcclusion quality thickness />`: creases, corners, the seam where a wall meets the floor and the ground
  under a statue darken where the room's light can't reach, which seats things in the scene. It darkens indirect light
  only (an `<AmbientLight>`, an `<Environment>`), not a sun or a lamp, so it shows in scenes lit mostly by the room or
  the sky. `quality` "medium" (the default) is right for most shots, "high" for close-ups of carved stone; "ultra" costs
  about 1 ms a frame at 1080p. `thickness` (metres, 0.25) is how thick things are taken to be behind what's seen.
- `<AntiAliasing mode />`: how edges are smoothed. `"msaa"` (4x multisampling) is the default; with
  `<AmbientOcclusion>` it can't run, and `"smaa"` (morphological, high preset) takes over. `"fxaa"` is the cheapest
  and softest, `"none"` leaves stair-stepped edges for a hard pixel look. There's no temporal anti-aliasing: it
  blends in the frames before, so a frame rendered on its own wouldn't equal the same frame in play.
- `<ToneMapping mode exposure />`: how light maps to the screen. `"tony"` is the default (neutral, holds colour);
  `"aces"` is filmic and contrasty (darker, punchier); `"agx"` is soft and holds highlights; `"neutral"`,
  `"reinhard"` and `"none"` are there too. `exposure` is in stops: `+1` twice as bright, `-1` half.
- `<DepthOfField focal_distance aperture_f_stops mode max_circle_of_confusion_diameter />` inside the
  `<Camera3d>`, as Bevy has it, a component on the camera: a lens's depth of field. What's nearer or farther than
  `focal_distance` (metres, 10 by default) blurs. `aperture_f_stops` is the f-number: 1.4 dreamy, 2.8 cinematic, 8
  nearly sharp. Pull focus by animating `focal_distance`: it changes every frame, as the fov does.
- `<Look mode pixelSize theme color lift gain />`: the whole frame in a model look's grain (`bevy/assets`): `"site"`
  (raea.io's six greys, Bayer-dithered) or `"pixel"`, a cell to `pixelSize` pixels. Bloom, fog and depth of field
  happen inside the grain. `color` (0..1, 1 by default) is how much of each cell's hue its grey keeps, so emissive
  colours stay coloured. `lift` 0 keeps black black. Use it instead of a model's own `look` when the world should
  share the model's grain; raea's cat in `content/cat3d/cinematic.tsx` (in a raea
  checkout, not the release) is the worked example.
- `<Look mode="paint" />`: the frame as a flat editorial illustration. Every surface is lit by the suns
  (DirectionalLights only, and point lights that ask: `paint` below) in `bands` flat tones: lit is its own colour,
  turned from the sun its colour times `mid` (form shadow), in a cast shadow its colour times `shadow`; 4+ bands step
  the lit side. Cast shadows are cut hard, so they read as shapes: give it one sun and a tight `<Shadows distance
  firstCascade cascades={1} />`. Then every edge wanders `rag` pixels (`ragScale` across; `boil` frames re-seeds it),
  a fixed paper `grain` lies over it, `sky` (one colour or `[top, bottom]`) fills wherever nothing's drawn, and
  `palette` (up to 16 colours) snaps every pixel to the nearest. `bands`, `grain`, `rag` and the seed are keyed per
  frame; the rest is the first frame's, so it's one painting a composition. Light colours: a white surface takes
  exactly `mid`/`shadow` (`shadow="#b4b6bc" mid="#cfa7a2"` is ref-4's cool grey and warm pink).
  A PointLight or SpotLight with `paint` paints a band of its own colour where it reaches (a CRT's glow on a face):
  out to about `6 * sqrt(intensity / 900000)` metres on a surface facing it (`intensity={45000}` about 1.3 m; `range`
  and a spot's cone cut it shorter; `shadow_maps_enabled` gives it a hard shadow), the surface its own colour times the light's
  colour scaled to white's brightness, in place of the `mid`/`shadow` shade (on a sunlit surface it adds only its
  hue), and at about half that distance a band a quarter brighter. Lights without `paint` still change nothing, and
  at most 8 paint a frame: `<PointLight transform={Transform.fromXyz(0, 1.5, 0.5)} intensity={45000} color="#4a7dff" paint />`.
- `<Look mode="cartoon" />`: paint's cartoon preset: two bands (a fill and one blush shade, `shadow="#f2c7b8"`), a
  thick even outline round silhouettes (`outline` colour, `outlineWidth` px, 6), and the line boiling on twos (`boil`
  2, `rag` 1.5). Lines come where the depth steps by 4% or more. `content/anything/paint/demo.tsx` (in a raea
  checkout) is the worked example of paint (three shots, 16:9 and 9:16).

```tsx
<>
  <Camera3d transform={Transform.fromXyz(8, 10, 8).lookingAt([0, 1.4, 0])} projection={{ Perspective: { fov: (34 * Math.PI) / 180 } }} />
  <Look mode="paint" bands={3} shadow="#b4b6bc" mid="#cfa7a2" grain={0.35} rag={2.2} sky="#5b9497" />
  <DirectionalLight transform={Transform.fromXyz(-5, 3.2, 6).lookingAt([0, 0, 0])} illuminance={9600} shadow_maps_enabled />
  <Shadows distance={40} firstCascade={30} cascades={1} mapSize={4096} />
  {/* ... */}
</>
```
- `<Grade temperature tint saturation shadows midtones highlights vignette aberration />`: one colour grade over every
  scene, so a film of many shots looks of a piece. `shadows`/`midtones`/`highlights` each take `{saturation, contrast,
  gamma, gain, lift}` (1, 1, 1, 1, 0 keep it); `temperature` warms (+) or cools (-) by about 0.03 a step; `vignette` is
  0..1 or `{intensity, radius, smoothness, color}`; `aberration` 0.002–0.005 is a lens's fringe. Like every effect,
  it's each frame's own: keep one across a film so it looks of a piece, give a shot its own, or ramp it from the
  frame. `bench/rerender/film.tsx` and its `shots.tsx` (in a raea checkout) are the worked example: six shots, each
  with its own sky, fog, bloom, grade or depth of field, in one composition.

## Composition passes: leaving part of the frame out of an effect

The frame-wide effects (the `<Look>`s, `<Outline>`, `<Bloom>`, `<Grade>`) work on everything by default. To keep
something out of them, such as a website on a `<Screen>` that has to read as the crisp page it is while the character
in front of it stays painted, put it in its own pass and have the effects skip that pass:

- `pass="ui"` on a `<Mesh3d>`, `<Model>`, `<Screen>`, `<Character>` (its skin and hull), `<RichText>` or an `<Entity>`
  (everything inside it that doesn't name its own). Passes are just names. Everything else is in `"scene"`, and a
  piece can have at most 3 other passes. A part's pass is keyed per frame.
- `<Look mode="paint" skip={["ui"]} />`: the skipped pass's pixels come out as drawn, with no bands, rag, grain,
  palette, edge or strokes, and its surfaces keep their own materials. `passes={{ ui: { rag: 0, grain: 0.05, bands: 4,
  stroke: 0, palette: false } }}` gives a pass its own settings (`rag`, `grain`, `palette`, `bands`, `edge`, `stroke`,
  `saturate`, `wash`) instead of skipping it. On the "site" and "pixel" looks, `skip` leaves a pass out of the grain.
- `<Outline skip={["ui"]} />`: no lines on the skipped pass and no creases against it. A scene object's silhouette in
  front of it still draws, on the object.
- `<Bloom skip={["ui"]} />`: the skipped pass doesn't glow. `passes={{ ui: 0.5 }}` gives it half the glow.
- `<Grade skip={["ui"]} />`: no vignette and no colour fringes on it (`passes` takes a share, as Bloom's does). Under
  `<ToneMapping mode="none" />` its temperature and grading are held back too; on a tone-mapped camera they happen
  inside the tone curve and still apply.

A pixel's pass is the nearest surface's, so a character in front of the page is painted and the page behind it isn't.
Under `<DepthOfField>` the pass's edge blurs with the frame, so a blurred page gets no hard painted halo.
`sdk/raea/bench/bevy/passes` is the fixture, and `content/anything/intro/opening-build.tsx` in a raea
checkout (the site's screens under the film's look) is the worked example.

```tsx
<Look mode="paint" bands={3} grain={0.1} rag={0.5} skip={["ui"]} />
<Outline color="#2a2030" skip={["ui"]} />
<Bloom intensity={0.3} skip={["ui"]} />
<Grade vignette={0.2} aberration={0.01} skip={["ui"]} />
<Screen name="site" pass="ui" crt={false} resolution={[1280, 720]} size={[3.2]}>{/* the page */}</Screen>
<Character body="kid" pose={pose} />
```

Costs: a scene with any pass turns on the depth and normal prepasses and turns MSAA off, as `<Outline>` does. It adds
two full-frame passes to build the mask (up to 97 taps a pixel under depth of field), and a copy plus one pass for each
of Bloom and Grade that skips something. A scene with no pass pays nothing.

## The lens: fisheye and barrel

- `<Fisheye strength={0..1} fov={120} />`: bends the 3D like a fisheye lens, corner to corner (nothing goes black).
  `strength` 0 is the camera's own picture, pixel for pixel, so ramp it in and out on beats with `animate`. `fov` is
  how wide the camera opens up as the fisheye comes in (degrees; 100-150 for a real fisheye feel), `mode="stereographic"`
  is gentler at the edges.
- `<LensDistortion k1 k2 />`: barrel (`k1` 0.1-0.4) or pincushion (`k1` below 0), zoomed just enough that the corners
  stay filled.
- Both take `edges="black"` (to show where the lens looks past the picture; edge pixels by default), and every number
  animates per frame, unlike the effects above. The lens's vignette and colour fringes are `<Grade>`'s.
- The page (HTML over the 3D: titles, captions, kinetic type) is never bent: the lens is a pass over the 3D only. To
  put words through the lens, make them 3D (`Text3D`, or a picture on an `ImagePlane`).
- Ink outlines (`ToonMaterial outline`) are drawn before the lens, so a fisheye fattens them in the middle and thins
  them towards the edges (by about the lens's squeeze there).

## Motion blur

- `<MotionBlur shutterAngle={0.5} samples={4} />`: fast moves smear (0.5 is a film camera's 180-degree shutter; 1 a
  whole frame). It animates per frame, and a frame without the element has none, so `{fast ? <MotionBlur /> : null}`
  blurs only the whip. `kind="bevy"` swaps raea's shutter for Bevy's own blur, to compare the two.
- It blurs inside moving parts and whole-frame camera moves; a part's silhouette over a still background, and toon ink
  lines, stay sharp (Bevy's method).
- With it, each frame is drawn after the one before it, so a frame's blur is the same in a render, a seek and play.
  That costs a second draw a frame.

## Why

These are Bevy's own camera effects (Bloom, DistanceFog, VolumetricFog, Tonemapping, Exposure) on the scene's camera. Bloom turns
the camera HDR so bright parts can exceed white before they bloom.

## Common mistakes

- Bloom with nothing bright in the scene: nothing glows. Add emissive parts or raise `exposure`.
- `threshold={0}` with a light background: the whole frame goes milky.
- Fog `far` shorter than the distance to the subject: the subject disappears.
- A render a shot, to give each shot its own look, joined after with ffmpeg: every effect here is each frame's own,
  so put each shot in a `<Sequence>` with its effects and render the film once.
- Fog volumes that show as boxes, or stair-stepped shafts: that's `mode="march"` (its `ambient` lights each box
  whole; too few `steps` step). Drop the mode: the grid has neither.
- A third shaft with a hard edge: only two spots and two directional lights are hero lights; the rest are lit in the
  grid's cells, softer. Put the shaft that matters on one of the first two.
- Glass in front of a hero shaft: the shaft in front of it is dimmed by the glass's opacity (the hero light is
  integrated to the solid surface behind).
- A `volumetric` light with no `<VolumetricFog>` or outside every `<FogVolume>`: no shaft. The fog volume has to
  contain the air the light crosses, and the camera's view of it.
- `<AmbientOcclusion>` in a scene lit only by a DirectionalLight or spots: nothing changes. It shades indirect light;
  add an AmbientLight or an Environment.
- Expecting `<AntiAliasing mode="msaa" />` next to `<AmbientOcclusion>`: SMAA is used instead (ambient occlusion
  can't multisample). SMAA can't recover sub-pixel detail as MSAA does: very thin wires and far railings shimmer more.
- `aces` making brand colours muddy: check a still against the kit; `tony` keeps colours closer.
- Text on the page expected to bend with a Fisheye: the page stays straight; make it 3D.
- MotionBlur on a part that only turns slowly: nothing shows. It reads on whips, spins and fast passes.
- Easing the whole look off so a page reads crisp (`rag`/`grain` to 0 as the site comes in): that unpaints the
  character too. Put the page in a pass (`<Screen pass="ui">`) and `skip={["ui"]}` on the effects instead.
- More than 3 passes besides "scene": the rest are drawn in "scene" (a warning says which).

## Example: a neon sign in fog

```tsx
import { AbsoluteFill, Composition, registerRoot, useCurrentFrame } from "raea";
import { Bloom, Fog, Text3D, ToneMapping } from "raea/3d";
import { LinearRgba, Srgba } from "raea/color";
import { StandardMaterial } from "raea/pbr";
import { Cuboid, Mesh3d } from "raea/mesh";
import { AmbientLight } from "raea/light";
import { Transform } from "raea/transform";
import { Camera3d } from "raea/camera";

function Neon() {
  const f = useCurrentFrame();
  const flicker = f % 37 === 0 ? 1 : 6; // a flicker on fixed frames, never random
  return (
    <AbsoluteFill style={{ background: "#07080c" }}>
      <Camera3d transform={Transform.fromXyz(0, 0.4, 6).lookingAt([0, 0.2, 0])} projection={{ Perspective: { fov: (45 * Math.PI) / 180 } }} />
      <AmbientLight brightness={40} />
      <Bloom intensity={1.6} threshold={0.9} />
      <Fog color="#07080c" near={5} far={14} />
      <ToneMapping mode="agx" />
      <Mesh3d transform={Transform.fromXyz(0, 0.4, 0)}>
        <Text3D size={0.7} depth={0.1}>OPEN</Text3D>
        <StandardMaterial base_color="#1a1a1a" emissive={LinearRgba.from(Srgba.hex("#ff2d75")).mul(flicker)} />
      </Mesh3d>
      {[0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map((i) => (
        <Mesh3d key={i} transform={Transform.fromXyz((i - 2) * 2.2, -0.6, -2 - i * 2.5)}>
          <Cuboid half_size={[0.3, 1, 0.3]} />
          <StandardMaterial base_color="#2a2f3a" perceptual_roughness={0.8} />
        </Mesh3d>
      ))}
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
}

registerRoot(() => <Composition id="neon" component={Neon} width={1280} height={720} fps={30} durationInFrames={60} />);
```

## Fire

`<Fire name position scale intensity color seed speed opacity light />` is a fire standing in the scene: a flame drawn
as a volume, its tongues quick at the foot and slow above, curling and tearing off into licks, every pixel a function of the frame (rising 3D noise inside
a tapering flame), so a render of any frame equals its play. It isn't a picture on a card: it has depth, the camera can
circle it, and with an `<AmbientOcclusion>` (which brings a depth pass) a log or a wall inside its box hides the flame
behind it.

- `position` is the flame's foot: stand it on its fuel (the top of a pyre's lowest logs, the bowl of a brazier).
- `scale` is its height in metres (half as wide), or `[width, height, depth]`. Keep it fixed; grow a fire by its
  `intensity`, since its tongues' speed depends on its height.
- `intensity` is how bright its core is, in the units of a material's emissive multiplier (`LinearRgba ... .mul(k)`). At night or indoors 6-15; a pyre
  roaring in the dark 20-35. Its hottest few percent is a white-yellow core well past 1, which a `<Bloom>` blooms.
  Too high and the whole flame goes to the core and reads white; small fires want less (a pit fire 4-6).
- `opacity` (1 by default) is how much of what's behind it the flame's body hides. Fire is light added over what's
  behind it, so it reads best against the dark (night sky, shadow, a dark doorway) and pales in front of a brightly
  lit surface; `opacity={1.5}` to `{3}` gives it a darker body there.
- `color` is the body's colour ("#ff7a1f"); the edges go deep red, the core yellow. `seed` makes fires differ;
  `speed` (1) scales how fast the tongues rise; `time` (seconds) overrides the Sequence's.
- `light` (1 by default; 0 for none) is a flickering PointLight at a third of its height, its flicker a function of
  the time. Turn it off when the scene has its own firelight. Mind the distance to what's behind the fire: a light of
  1 gives 8000 lux at 3 m but about 110,000 at 0.8 m, which turns a wall just behind the flame white, and an additive
  flame over white disappears. For a brazier against a wall, put the light on the camera's side of the flame at a few
  hundredths (Rome's street altar: 0.05, 0.6 m in front of the bowl).
- Put embers (small emissive spheres on seeded paths) and smoke (a `<FogVolume>` starting just above the flame's tips,
  not around it: fog in front of the flame hides it) round it yourself.

```tsx
<Fire name="pyre" position={[0, 0.2, 24]} scale={[2.6, 5, 2]} intensity={10 + 25 * burn} speed={0.9} opacity={2} light={0} />
```

Cost: a fire is a box whose pixels each march 32 samples (`steps`), so it costs by its area on screen: about 1 ms a
frame at 1920x1080 for a fire filling a third of the frame (the fixture's pyre, measured as the difference between
48 and 240 steps), far less for one in the distance. For several big fires in play, lower `steps` (16-24).

## Clouds, smoke and contrails in the light

`<Cloud>`, `<Smoke>` and `<Contrail>` are fluids simulated on a grid and ray-marched, and they take part in the
scene's light as a mesh does: each is drawn into the lights' shadow maps, so it throws soft shadows on the ground,
meshes and models under it that move as it drifts and billows, and the volumetric fog, which walks the same maps,
shows the sun's shafts breaking through the gaps between clouds (god rays). No extra component is needed:

- Shafts need a `volumetric` DirectionalLight, a `<VolumetricFog>` (march or froxel) and a `<FogVolume>` of haze
  round the clouds and under them. A low sun behind the clouds from the camera shows the shafts best.
- The shadow is where the volume has stopped half the sun: its dense body, not its faint wisps. `shadow` on a volume
  (on by default) scales the density it sees: `1` as drawn, more reaches into thinner parts (a fatter shadow; up to
  `4`, a thin contrail's made to show), less keeps to the dense cores, `false` none. Under a paint look the shadow is
  the painted shape.
- Soften the shadow's edge with the sun's `softShadow` (2-4 for clouds): a cloud far above its shadow gets a wide soft
  edge, as a real one does.
- The shadows fall where the sun's cascades reach (`<Shadows distance>`); a cloud far above still casts into them.
- A shape that should only block the light, never be seen, is `<Mesh3d shadow="only">` (a roof out of frame, a blind's
  slats cutting the shafts).

```tsx
<DirectionalLight name="sun" transform={Transform.fromXyz(50, 75, -185).lookingAt([0, 0, 0])} illuminance={48000} volumetric shadow_maps_enabled soft_shadow_size={2} />
<VolumetricFog mode="froxel" />
<FogVolume name="haze" position={[0, 10, -10]} scale={[120, 24, 120]} density={0.025} scattering={0.5} anisotropy={0.7} />
<Cloud name="mid" position={[3 + drift, 16, -20]} size={[14, 7, 8]} seed={4} time={t + 5} />
<Cloud name="thin" position={[19 + drift, 13, -12]} size={[12, 6, 8]} seed={9} time={t + 3} shadow={0.7} />
```

Every value is from the frame (the field at the volume's time), so a frame alone
equals that frame in play. The fixture is `sdk/raea/bench/bevy/volume-light`.

# Scene and camera The 3D names are Bevy's: a part is an entity with a `transform`, a camera is a `Camera3d`, a mesh a `Mesh3d` with its shape and material inside it. Import them from the module Bevy keeps them in: `raea/camera`, `raea/transform`, `raea/mesh` (with the shapes), `raea/pbr`, `raea/light` (or everything from `raea/prelude`). `Entity` (and `Canvas3D`, for `layered`) come from `raea/3d`. ## What to do - Write the camera, lights and meshes straight in the page, inside an `AbsoluteFill` like any element; no wrapper is needed. The element holding the camera is cleared to show the 3D, and its `background` (a hex colour) becomes the 3D's clear colour. A gradient background doesn't reach the 3D (it clears to black); use a flat colour, or a large backdrop mesh. - A camera in an element smaller than the frame draws its view in that element's box, over the element's background (an inset monitor, a picture in picture); the page around the box is the page alone. - Give it one ``. Place it with a `Transform`: `Transform.fromXyz(x, y, z)` puts it there, `.lookingAt([x, y, z])` turns it to face that point (without one it faces -Z). The projection is `{{ Perspective: { fov } }}`, the vertical field of view in radians: `(40 * Math.PI) / 180` reads as a product lens, 60 degrees or more as wide. The y axis is up, and +z points at the viewer. - Move the camera by computing its transform from the frame: a dolly is `z` easing from 8 to 5, an orbit is `Transform.fromXyz(r * Math.sin(a), h, r * Math.cos(a)).lookingAt([0, 0, 0])`. Both are drawn exactly per frame in render and play. - Use `` for things that move together (a product on a turntable, a car and its wheels): its children are placed in it, as Bevy's child entities are. Entities nest; their transforms compose. Turn one with `Transform.IDENTITY.withRotation(Quat.fromEuler("XYZ", x, y, z))` (radians). - 2D under the 3D: put the 3D in a ``. The 3D then takes its place in the page's tree order: - Page elements before the Canvas3D, and the background of the box holding it, are under the 3D. They show wherever it has nothing and are hidden by its parts. - Positioned elements after it are over it. - The 3D's background is transparent, so a gradient or a picture behind the 3D works. - Put the layered Canvas3D straight in a full-frame `AbsoluteFill`. Give the elements after it a position (`AbsoluteFill`, `position: absolute`): as in CSS, positioned elements paint over unpositioned ones. - Put 2D over the 3D as ordinary page elements after the 3D. Keep page parts over the 3D opaque: a partly transparent part over 3D blends a little differently in a render than in play (a known engine difference), so fade text in over a flat panel rather than over the 3D, or accept a slight mismatch while it fades. ```tsx // 2D behind and in front of the 3D: a disc and a word under the sphere, a bar over it
``` ## Why The camera and the entities are rows the engine reads each frame, keyed per frame, so a camera move is as exact as a title's slide. Entities are composed into world space before the engine sees them. ## Common mistakes - `Quat.fromEuler("XYZ", 0, 90, 0)`: radians. Use `Math.PI / 2`. - `fov: 40`: radians too, so 40 is a fisheye past anything a lens does. Write `(40 * Math.PI) / 180`. - The camera at the subject's position, or looking away from it: nothing shows. Start at `Transform.fromXyz(0, 1, 6).lookingAt([0, 0, 0])` and adjust. - `.lookingAt` a point straight above or below the camera: there's no up to turn by. Look a little off vertical. - Two cameras to cut between angles. Use one camera whose transform jumps at the cut frame. - `useFrame` or refs from react-three-fiber on raea's own components: there's no render loop for them. Write the frame's values as props. An R3F scene goes inside ``, where they work (`bevy/r3f`). - 2D meant to pass behind a 3D part, without a ``: otherwise the whole page is over the 3D. - An unpositioned element after a layered Canvas3D: it paints under the 3D (CSS paints positioned boxes last). Make it `position: absolute`. - Bloom with `layered`: its glow lightens the page under the 3D around bright parts (it adds light there). ## Example: a product on a turntable with a slow push-in and a title over it ```tsx import { AbsoluteFill, Composition, Easing, interpolate, registerRoot, useCurrentFrame, useVideoConfig } from "raea"; import { Cylinder, Entity } from "raea/3d"; import { StandardMaterial } from "raea/pbr"; import { Cuboid, Mesh3d } from "raea/mesh"; import { AmbientLight, DirectionalLight } from "raea/light"; import { Quat, Transform } from "raea/transform"; import { Camera3d } from "raea/camera"; function Turntable() { const f = useCurrentFrame(); const { fps, durationInFrames } = useVideoConfig(); const turn = (f / fps) * (Math.PI / 3); // a sixth of a turn a second const z = interpolate(f, [0, durationInFrames - 1], [7, 5], { easing: Easing.out(Easing.cubic), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp" }); return (

# Whole scenes: brief, build, review, judge

A believable scene is planned before it is modelled, built big to small with a measured check after every step, and
reviewed from the same fixed cameras every round by a judge that has never seen the code. This is the loop the people
who make striking Blender scenes with an agent use (the 11-06 research: dream-loop, AnyScene, kiln, prasenx,
hayashimon, KOBATAKA), each step on a raea verb.

## What to do

The brief template, the builder prompt and the judge prompt to paste are in `bevy/prompts`. A kit of props is
`bevy/kits`; shooting a finished set is `bevy/shots`.

### 0. The job: `make` on brief.ts, held by `raea make status`

- Put the job on the brief: `make: scene({ references, style, dials, objects })` from `raea/brief`. Each object has
  one size (`h`, `dims` or `max`), a `route`, `source: "reference" | "invented"` and, in a scene, `at` and `rot`
  (metres from the floor's front-left corner; rot 0 faces the entrance). Dials you don't set are read from the
  reference, so set only the ones the person asked for (`source: "customer"`).
- `raea make status` decides in code whether you're done: the deliverables on disk, every gate, the judge's rounds.
  The Stop hook asks it at the end of every turn, and you can't stop while it says "not done" (the loop gives way at
  the 8-round cap, on a stall, or when the same thing is missing three turns running). `--plan` writes the gates as
  check lines under the job's task in plan.org.
- `raea make plan` is the stop before anything costs money: `review/plan/floor-plan.png` (every footprint, invented
  ones dashed), a grey-box blockout seen from the entrance with its review sheets, and `comparison.png` beside the
  reference. Show it, fix positions and sizes, and only then generate.
- NOTES.md beside the brief ends with `## What the skill got wrong`: what the guides or tools led you into. Status
  checks it's there once the work is.

### 1. The brief: a picture, a size, and what not to add

- `brief.ts` (`brief()` from `raea/brief`) holds one place, one time, one look:
  - `look`: three to five mood words, plus the real thing it must look like ("film stills of a 1990s Tokyo
    laundromat", never "a game").
  - `references`: the target, which is a "real in-engine screenshot" of the scene from hero camera 1
    (`raea gen image "..." --aspect 16:9 -o media/ref`), and real photos of the kind of place, used for judging only.
  - `notDoing`: the do-not-add list (weather, time of day, people, UI, real brands). Without it the agent adds rain
    and neon.
  - `sections`:
    - Space: real metres. Real places are small; a shop is 3.5 x 6 m.
    - Zones.
    - Hero cameras: position, target, lens.
    - Practicals: each real light source and its kelvin.
    - Objects: one row per object, `id | what | real size m | route | faces | seen from m`.
    - Wear.
    - Printed matter.
    - Motion.
    - Budget: generation cents and judge rounds.
- Each hero object gets a `NAME.parts.ts` (`parts()`) with its concept (what, style, size, seenFrom, material) and parts, each
  with a role, a level (primary, secondary, tertiary), a parent, a count and `near` detail. Below it, add a connection
  map with one line per joint: `door <-> cabinet  hinge side  touches`.
- Write the plan from how the real thing is built: look up the product, the catalogue or a drawing.

### 2. Route every object: which tool makes which kind of thing

Ask one question of each object: **is it defined by numbers, by a rule, or by its looks?**
- **Numbers** (sizes, a hole that must fit, a hinge line): Manifold solids, or `raea/room` for the shell.
- **A rule** (a blend of bodies, a branching, a field of copies): `sdf.*`, `grow.*`, `<Instances>`.
- **Its looks** (a worn tool, a lamp, food, anything with character): `raea gen` or a CC0 library model.

The TSX is always the scene. Blender is only a workshop an asset passes through on its way into `media/`, when a
check names a script (`bevy/blender`). It never places, lights, frames, materials or animates the scene.

| the object | made by | then in Blender when |
|---|---|---|
| **numbers**: walls, counters, shelves, boxes, frames, pipes, sign boards, anything a hinge must fit | Manifold solids (`manifold.*`, `<Mesh3d shape={solid}>`, `bevy/meshes`) | it needs real UVs or baked AO (`raea solid info` names bake.py when the file's `needs.textured` is set), a cloth falls on it (cloth.py), or a fillet solids can't make: `raea solid export` first, and log the gap |
| **numbers**: the room shell, runs of cabinets, openings, hung decor | `raea/room` (`bevy/rooms`) | never |
| **a rule**: a creature, a limb, a handle grown from a body, a melted or poured form | `sdf.*` fields with smooth unions, `.solid()` (`bevy/meshes`, "Organic shapes and growth") | it must bend (rig.py, after `raea solid export`) |
| **a rule**: too many or too organic to place by hand: trees, terrain, boulders, succulents, a vase's profile | `grow.tree`, `grow.terrain`, `grow.boulder`, `grow.rosette`, `grow.loft` | never |
| **a rule**: a lawn, a meadow, a field of copies | `<Grass>`, `<Instances>` with `scatter()` (`bevy/meshes`) | never |
| **looks**, seen close (under about 2 m) or a hero: appliances, tools, electronics, crockery, food | `raea gen` mesh, `tripo:H3.1` (`motion/gen`) | `raea gen check` names a script: over the triangle budget for `--seen` (decimate.py), debris or holes (repair.py), one blob where `--parts` names moving parts (split.py), no skeleton with `--rig` (rig.py) |
| **looks**, seen far, to be edited or rigged, or numerous | `raea gen` mesh, `tripo:P2` (quads) | the same checks; P2's quads rig better |
| **looks**: an exact real asset exists under CC0 (Poly Haven, ambientCG) | `<Model>` (`bevy/assets`) | it's FBX, OBJ or .blend (convert.py), or heavier than its distance needs (decimate.py) |
| far background | a generated picture on an `ImagePlane` | never |

- Every generated row carries its real height, and for boxy things its dims (generators invent depth):
  `raea gen mesh "..." --h 0.9 --turn 0` measures the model and fits it on the way in (`raea gen check` reports
  size, facing, pivot, pieces and triangles).
- A reference picture for each generated prop uses the scan template: *Studio product photograph of a single real
  object, photorealistic, true colours, [condition], soft even diffused light, plain pale grey seamless background,
  the whole object in frame with margin, three-quarter view from slightly above, sharp focus, no people, no text, no
  brand names, no logos.*

### 3. Build, one stage at a time; a stage that fails its check is fixed first

0. **Plan.** Every object row has a route and a real size, and every hero has a `NAME.parts.ts`.
1. **Space.** Block the room as boxes at real size. Place furniture by relations, not typed coordinates:
   `place({ room, objects, rules })` from raea/3d. Rules are `on`, `against` a wall, `beside`, `near`, `apart`,
   `facing`, `align` and `clear` (floor kept free in front). It returns each object's `center`, `base` and `yaw`,
   plus `found` for whatever couldn't hold. Check: `raea run checks.ts` with `checkLayout(plan)` prints no
   errors. Then review it in clay (step R).
2. **Generate in bulk, early.** Put every generated row in one flow:
   - Quote it first with `raea gen plan props.flow.ts`.
   - Run it in the background with `raea gen run props.flow.ts -o media/gen`.
   - Look at every reference picture before its mesh runs.
3. **Objects, big to small.** Go in this order:
   - Furniture, then heroes, then mid-size things, then clutter. Block each one out at its planned bounds first.
   - Then work each part through its levels: silhouette, then structure, then detail.
   - Build ONE of a repeated thing, check it, then pattern it.
   - After each object, run `raea scene lint EDIT.tsx --json --part ID`. It must show nothing floating, sunk or
     clipping. Apply its `{y, dy}` fixes in code, never by eye. Each joint in the connection map must touch.
4. **Light, practicals first.** Give every practical its real kelvin, and add fills last, weak.
   - Check with `raea scene light EDIT.tsx --part HERO --json`.
   - Read the EXPOSURE line `raea render` prints for every still. It gives mean luma, the 1st and 99th percentiles,
     what clips and what crushes, and the stops from mid grey.
5. **Surfaces.** Give every material one wear recipe, at different strengths: chipped edges, dirt in gaps, dust on
   tops, grime at the floor line (`ProceduralExtension`'s `dust`, `dirt` and `edges`, or `WearExtension` on paint; see `bevy/materials`). Leave nothing a
   flat default colour. Lay out printed matter as a 2D composition, render it to a PNG, use the PNG as the map, then
   age it.
6. **Motion, last and small.** First `raea scene stage EDIT.tsx`: it steps every frame without drawing and holds it
   to the checks the render fails on (3D words too small or turned too far to read, a part that snaps, a camera that
   lurches or goes in and back out, frames with almost nothing on screen). A sign nobody is meant to read takes
   `read={false}`. Then `raea render EDIT.tsx -o out/scene.mp4` and `raea check out/scene.mp4`.
   - Once things move, check how they move. Render with `--layers`, and render `--aov -o out/scene.aov` beside it for
     depth. Then run `raea fingerprint things out/scene.mp4 --json > things.json` and
     `raea check out/scene.mp4 --things things.json`. It finds a thing floating or passing through another, the
     camera lurching mid-move, and an empty frame.

### R. Review after every stage and every fix

- Run `raea render EDIT.tsx --review review/rN`. It renders the same fixed cameras every round, computed from the
  scene's bounds and written to `review/rN/cameras.json`: hero (the scene's own camera), front, right, top, iso, and
  low at 0.3 m.
- Each camera is rendered in colour and in clay (every material light grey, so form and assembly are judged without
  surfaces).
- The cameras are stitched into `colour.png` and `clay.png`, with a JSON sidecar of the tiles and their exposure.
  `--clay` alone renders any frame in clay.
- Open the sheets and look at every tile yourself. "Looks good" is not a review. Name each problem with its tile and
  its fix, for example "the dryer doors are flat grey discs".
- Hand the sheets to the judge (below). Fix every blocking defect it names, or write down why it is wrong and what
  you checked.
- Change one thing per material per round. Re-run the stage's checks after every fix.

### The judge, and the gates

Three tiers, each gating once it has earned it (`raea make status` lists them):

1. **Measured checks always gate:** `raea scene lint` (floats and sinks at the feet, clips with the move that clears
   them, faces z-fighting in one plane), `raea gen check` on every generated model, `raea scene stage --clearance 0.45` on
   a moving camera, and the deliverables' counts.
2. **`raea ask` questions gate one at a time, once calibrated.** The make set (`raea ask SHEET --set make`, or the
   command status prints) asks yes/no about one sheet: floating, intersecting, blobby, a stand-in, flat colour,
   plastic, opaque glass, garbled hero text, a real brand, too dark or bright; on a reference sheet, an outlier, two
   objects, a brand; on a framing sheet, a camera through a wall or a subject lost. Every answer lands in the ask
   ledger, matched to the sheet's bytes, so a re-rendered sheet needs asking again. A question gates once
   `raea ask calibrate` passes it (16 problem and 16 clean labels, held-out AUC 0.8); until then it's advice in the
   status.
3. **A fresh critic for the fixes.** `raea judge review/rN --kind scene --by claude --brief brief.ts --target
   media/ref/target.png --json` (or clef, kimi) scores the kind's rubric (scene: layout, props, signage, materials,
   light, atmosphere, plausibility, composition; layout and props judged on clay), on a production bar: don't
   nitpick, at most five fixes. It sees the sheets and the brief's words only, never the code or your log. Code
   decides the pass; the thresholds aren't in the prompt. A round judged on another kind's rubric doesn't count.
   Fix every blocking defect it names, or answer it in NOTES.md (its words, then what you checked). Its score gates
   once `raea judge calibrate --kind scene` agrees with Shane's eye (`raea judge eye`).

### Stopping

`raea make status` says it; you don't decide it.

- **Done:** every deliverable on disk, every gate clear, and two fresh critic passes in a row on the latest renders.
- **Stall:** three rounds without beating the best score, or the same defect named twice. Stop tweaking and change
  the approach for that part: another route (solid, field, Tripo HD, Meshy), a rebuilt light plan, or a moved camera.
  A defect that comes back after two fixes belongs to the method, not the dose.
- **Cap:** 8 critic rounds a job. At the cap or a stall the job is delivered short: status lists what's still
  missing, and the Stop hook lets you end with it said.

## Why

- Fixed cameras and a clay pass are what every strong source judges on. Colour hides bad form, and a moving camera
  hides regressions.
- A judge that has seen the code grades the intent, not the pixels. A judge that knows the pass line gets gamed.
- Measured checks (lint, light, exposure, gen check) catch what eyes miss: a 3 cm float, a fridge at 4 m tall, a
  frame two stops under.

## Common mistakes

- Modelling the hero from primitives when it has character: route it to Tripo HD, or to a field if it is organic.
- Placing generated models by nudging transforms: fit them on the way in (`--h`, `--turn`), then lint.
- Several fixes to light and materials at once: they are coupled, so do one a round.
- Calling a stage done because the command ran: every claim needs an image or a check's output.
