# The floor

Read this right before you edit a composition, every time, even for a one-line change. The floor isn't a style. It
lists what breaks a piece, plus the habits that have already been corrected once. Each line here came from a real
note on real work. When the person's taste file (`~/.raea/taste/`) says otherwise, the taste file wins.

Work through it on one render, not one line at a time. Pull stills at the moments that matter, look at them together,
fix everything they show, then render and look again.

## Verify

Before you say a piece is done, every line here is true of the last render, not of the code:

- **Text fits.** No word runs off the frame, off its card or into the next line. Text that has to be read is at
  least 60 px at 1080 wide (scale with width), with at least 3:1 contrast against the pixels behind each glyph.
- **Text stays out of the app's buttons.** In a vertical frame with the platform unknown, keep the top 220 px, the
  bottom 420, the right 140 and the left 60 clear (TikTok: top 108, bottom 320, right 120; Reels: top 210, bottom 310,
  right 84; Shorts: top 120, bottom 300, right 96). A 4:5 feed frame needs top 110, bottom 170, sides 60; a 1:1 frame
  top 70, bottom 120, sides 60; 16:9 top and bottom 120, sides 60. These zones are only where text can't go. Where it
  should go is a design choice.
- **Nothing flashes past the limit.** No more than three flashes in any one second over a sizable part of the frame
  (WCAG 2.3.1): past that, flashing can cause seizures. A strobe or a fast flicker needs slowing, shrinking or less contrast.
- **Cues land on their words.** A cut, a move or a caption tied to speech starts on the word, timed from the
  transcript's word times. Never place one by eye or at a fixed tempo.
- **Every name the voice says is on screen when it says it.** If the narration says "the brief", the brief is visible.
- **Nothing stands still for three seconds** unless the stillness is the point. A held frame needs a reason the viewer
  can feel.
- **Reading time.** About 0.3 s a word, and at least a second for anything that has to be read, counted while it can
  be read: faded, covered or lost against its ground doesn't count, and `raea check` says which frames were lost. A
  number gets time to land before the next thing replaces it.
- **The mix.** -14 LUFS integrated (±1), true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and the voice clear over everything.
  Changing the target needs the person's say-so.
- **Names are spelled right.** People, products and places are spelled as the brief has them, never as the
  transcript heard them.
- **You looked.** You have seen the frames at the moments that matter, at the size it ships, and opened the whole
  export, not just a shot.
- **A note got its move.** Before any edit for a note, you picked the move it asks for (`raea guide router` lists
  them) and read that move's guide (`raea guide layout`, `raea guide quieter`, ...).
- **The last version is still there.** Each version renders to a new file beside the old (`card-v2.mp4` next to
  `card.mp4`), never over it, and in the app it's posted naming the item it `replaces`.

## Refuse

Each of these was corrected once. Don't make the same mistake twice. One is allowed only when the brief or the
direction asks for it by name, and the direction then says why in a line.

- **Close-ups with no reason.** A cut to a detail has to answer something the viewer just wondered about.
- **Wide, empty shots.** Frame close or medium on a subject: a person, a product, the thing that's happening.
- **Labels written into the 3D.** Words that name or point at a part are a `Label`: page type over the scene, sized in
  pixels of the frame, placed through the shot's camera. Words in the world are only what's really there (a sign, a page in a book), and `raea render` fails on
  any it can't read: too small, turned past 50°, behind a part or never fully revealed (`bevy` rule 9). A part a
  `Label` names is what the shot is about, so it fails when the frame's edge cuts that part (`subject-cut`).
- **A 3D film rendered a shot at a time.** Render the film whole. A frame looks the same however it's reached, and
  `raea render` renders a sample of a film's frames again alone and fails on one that differs (`frame-pure`). A shot a
  process works round an engine fault; when one shows, report it with `raea bug` instead of building round it.
- **Cameras that ease from A to B and stop.** A camera keeps moving at the start and end of a shot, so cuts join
  motion to motion. Stop only when following a subject that stops.
- **Cutting to a constant tempo.** Cut to the song's map (its beats, downbeats, builds and drops), never to a BPM
  times a bar count.
- **Effects stacked until the work blurs.** Bloom, grain, blur, glow and lens tricks that soften or de-rez what the
  piece is about. One effect, used where it means something.
- **Glow on everything.** Light is a cue: it pulses where the eye should go and nowhere else.
- **Drawn highlights where a cursor should act.** In a walkthrough, a real cursor moves and clicks; outlines and
  boxes don't stand in for it.
- **A tour of features.** Follow one project through one loop. A list of capabilities isn't a story.
- **A random script.** Plan it first (who it's for, the one belief, then a storyboard) instead of writing lines
  for whatever is on screen.
- **Template captions.** White bold text with one yellow word, an emoji pop, a zoom on every sentence, a whoosh on
  every entrance.
- **The same move everywhere.** One entrance, one zoom or one sound on every beat makes every beat weaker.
- **Music by default.** A bed under every second, or a held pad and drone standing in for a score. Decide what each
  scene is heard as, and compose what it needs (`motion/music`).
- **Copy that sounds like an ad.** Buzzwords, "Not X. Y." cadences, aphorisms, a label above every headline.

## Never

No reason makes these right:

- **Invented facts.** No number, result, price, quote, customer or comparison that the brief, the person or the
  footage didn't give you. If the piece needs proof you don't have, make it without the proof and say what would help.
- **Generated images or video.** Pictures come from real footage, stock in the project's media, or are built:
  components, drawn shapes, 3D. Generated sound is allowed: TokenSynth instruments, SAO foley and Pocket TTS
  narration (all local).
- **Redrawn logos.** Use the real files.
- **Calling it done without looking.** A render nobody looked at isn't finished.

# Mode: play

Games and playable scenes: pieces whose job is that someone wants another go.

## It works when

A new player understands what to do within two seconds of looking, their first input does something they can see
and hear, and when it ends they press to play again.

## What to make

- **It plays live.** A game always runs live on the stage, never as a video in its place. If it's too slow, fix the
  cost, not the liveness.
- **Readable in two seconds.** The player, the goal and the danger read at a glance: by shape and contrast first,
  colour second. One look should tell you what you are.
- **The first input answers.** The first key or touch moves something, with a sound. A screen that ignores the
  player loses them.
- **Feel before features.** Get the core move right (its speed, weight, sound, and the frame it lands on) before
  adding a second one.
- **Clear failure, quick restart.** The player sees why they lost and is playing again in a moment.
- **Deterministic.** State lives in `useGameState` with a pure step, so a logged play renders back to the same pixels.

## The decisions

- **The core move and its numbers.** Set the speed, the acceleration, how long a jump hangs and the frame where it
  lands. The easy default is whatever the physics gives you. Tune the numbers by hand while you play.
- **What the camera shows.** Show what the player needs to see coming. The easy default is a fixed camera centred
  on the player, which hides the danger on a fast run toward the edge of the screen.
- **The first minute.** Let the first obstacle teach the move. The easy default is a line of instructions.
- **The run and the restart.** Decide how long a run lasts and how quickly the player is back in after losing. Both
  should be short enough that one more go is easy to say yes to.
- **Sound.** Give every input and every outcome a sound (`games`). Silence after a jump reads as a missed jump.
- **What is random.** Seed it from the game's state, so a logged play renders back the same.

## The rut

A title screen before anything happens. Controls explained in text instead of taught by the first obstacle. A score
that means nothing.

## How it fails

| What you see | Why | What to change |
|---|---|---|
| new players stand still | the goal or the player doesn't stand out | separate them by shape and contrast first, then by colour |
| the controls feel floaty or stiff | the feel numbers were never tuned: slow acceleration, no landing frame | tune them live, one at a time |
| deaths feel unfair | the cause wasn't visible: a hitbox bigger than the sprite, danger off screen | make hitboxes match the drawing, and show danger before it arrives |
| a replay doesn't match the play | some state lives outside `useGameState`: `Math.random()`, the clock, a ref | move it into the step, seeded from state (`harden`) |
| it stutters live | the frame costs too much | reduce the cost (`optimize`). Never swap in a video |

## Check

- Playtest it live, with real input, not from a rendered video.
- Harden the edges: two keys at once, holding a key, losing focus, the very first frame and the last.

# How a piece is judged

A critique has three parts, and the person sees all three on one test item in the feed:

1. **Measured.** `raea check` on the export: clipped text, text under a platform's buttons, captions too brief to
   read, caption contrast, frozen stretches, flashing past the limit, cues off their words, loudness, blotching in the darks. These are facts;
   a P0 or P1 among them is never argued with.
2. **Judged.** The decision model watches the export (its first minute, with sound) and rates it on the questions
   below, each on five levels: poor, weak, acceptable, strong, excellent. It reads the brief's facts and the
   storyboard's logline first, so it judges this piece for these people, not pieces in general.
3. **Written.** The agent turns every judged answer under "acceptable" into an issue the person can act on: the
   moment, what the viewer meets there, and the move that fixes it (`retime`, `clarify`, `regrade`...). It names the
   strongest moment too, so polish leaves it alone.

## The questions

Each line is `id (modes it applies to): the question`. `all` means every mode. A question that doesn't apply to a
piece's modes isn't asked.

- open (pitch, story, explain): In the first two seconds, is there a picture, a word or a sound that would make this audience stop, and does it raise something the rest of the piece answers?
- point (all): After one watch, could this audience say what the piece wants them to believe in one plain sentence?
- shown (pitch, explain): When the narration claims something, is the thing on screen at that moment, working, rather than only described?
- loop (explain): Does it follow one project through one loop, each step leading to the next, without jumping between unrelated examples?
- pull (story): Does each scene end on something unresolved, so this audience wants the next one?
- land (pitch, story, explain): Does the end land: something this audience can do next, a payoff, or a return to the opening?
- pace (all): Do shot lengths change with what they hold, with no stretch sitting still longer than it earns, and cuts falling on words or beats?
- read (all): Is every word that matters large, sharp against what is behind it, and on long enough to read?
- sound (all): Is the voice clear over everything else, with music and effects marking moments rather than filling space, and any music written for this cut (a tune, harmony that moves, a rhythm, an ending on a cut) rather than a pad or drone held under it?
- sound-silent (silent): With no voice, do the music and the effects carry it: cuts and moments landing on the beat, the music composed (a tune, moving harmony, a rhythm, sections that change with the picture), each effect marking a moment rather than filling space, nothing muddy? (asked in place of sound when no one speaks)
- world (all): Do colour, type, motion and sound hold one direction from the first frame to the last?
- own (all): With the name covered, could this only be this project, rather than any product in its category?
- feel (play): Does the player's input change the picture right away and in a way they can read?
- again (play): After a failure, is it clear what went wrong and is the next attempt one press away?
- task (tool): Can the task the screen exists for be done without stopping to work out where to look?

## Music that sounds generated

Listen for these before the decision model does; each is how a made score gives itself away, and the fix
(`motion/music`):

- **One held texture.** A pad, a sine sub and a long reverb under everything, no attack anywhere. Write a motif, chords
  that move and a part with rhythm; reverb per instrument, nothing on the bus.
- **Harmony that stands still.** One chord for four bars or more in a cue that's meant to move. Change it every bar or two.
- **A loop, not a cue.** The same two bars for thirty seconds. Vary the motif, change the arrangement every four to
  eight bars, and turn where the edit turns.
- **Played by a machine.** Every note at one velocity, exactly on the grid. Spread the dynamics; move played parts a
  few milliseconds; use a recorded groove.
- **No ending.** A fade-out. End on a chord or a hit on the last cut.
- **Everywhere.** Music under every scene because the piece "needs music". Some scenes belong to silence or to their
  own sound.
- **The wrong source.** A whole score from TokenSynth takes (organ-like sustains, buzz) or from an SAO "ambient
  music" prompt. Recorded instruments play the parts; TokenSynth fills a timbre no library has; SAO makes effects.

## Ranking

| | Means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| **P0** | The piece fails: a floor defect, a wrong fact, the point doesn't come through | Fix before anything else |
| **P1** | This audience would stop watching or stop believing here | Fix in this pass |
| **P2** | It costs attention: a slow patch, a generic part, a mix fighting the voice | Fix if the pass has room |
| **P3** | Finishing: a few frames of timing, an alignment, a colour step | Fix last, or leave |

A judged answer of "poor" is P1, and P0 on `point` or on the mode's own first question (`open` for pitch, `loop` for
explain, `pull` for story, `feel` for play, `task` for tool). "weak" is P2. Measured findings keep `raea check`'s
rank. Torn between two ranks: would this audience leave at this moment? If yes, it's at least P1.

## Passing

A stage's gate opens when its latest critique has no P0 or P1 left. P2 and P3 go to `polish`, which works from the
latest critique and posts the next one.

# harden

Notes like these: "it broke when I…", "what if two people press", "it gets stuck", "edge case". A game's or a tool's
edges.

## Assess
- List the inputs nobody designed for: two keys at once, holding a key, pressing during a transition, losing focus,
  resizing, the very first frame and the last, a very long name, nothing at all.
- Reproduce the note's case first, live, with real input.

## Decide
- Which edges matter here. For a game, that's input and timing. For a tool, that's data and its states.
- What each case should do: ignore the input, queue it, or refuse with words that say why. Decide it in the step,
  once.

## Change
- Fix the cause in the pure step (`useGameState`), not a guard in the view.
- Every state has a picture: empty, loading, error, won, lost.
- Keep it deterministic, so a logged play renders back to the same pixels.

## Verify
- Play the case again live, then the cases next to it. Run the replay check.

## When it goes wrong
- A guard in the view hides the bug, and the replay no longer matches the play.
- The fix for the reported case breaks the case next to it. Play the neighbours too.
- An error state has no way out.

# optimize

Notes like these: "it's slow", "the file's too big", "it stutters", "the game lags", "it took forever to render".
The same piece, lighter: smaller files, faster renders, smooth play.

## Assess
- Measure first: the export's size and bitrate (`raea media probe`), the render's time, a game's frame rate live.
- Find the cost: footage at a far higher resolution than the frame, 3D lights and shadows nobody sees, a model with
  more triangles than pixels, per-frame work that could be computed once.

## Decide
- Which cost the note means: the file's size, the render's time or the game's frame rate. Each has its own fix.
- What may change. The look stays the same unless the person agrees to a trade.

## Change
- Delivery: `--quality` per use (`raea guide rendering`); a share copy for sending (the skill's ffmpeg line).
- Footage: `raea mezz` for long-GOP sources; trim to the parts used.
- 3D: fewer shadow-casting lights, smaller shadow maps, decimated models (`raea guide bevy/blender`), the limits in
  `raea guide bevy/limits`.
- Code: compute what doesn't change outside the frame function, keyed by index, still frame-pure.

## Verify
- The same measurements, before and after. The look is unchanged in stills at the same frames.

## When it goes wrong
- The look changed: banding in gradients, blotching in dark frames, soft detail from a bitrate set too low.
- The fix was guessed, not measured, and nothing got faster.
- Work cached outside the frame broke frame purity, so a render no longer matches its play.

# The person's fingerprint

A fingerprint is the person's sense of good work, as raea has learned it on their Mac from their notes, marks and
approvals: a list of axes (blur, a black frame, hiss, clipping, a glow over everything, a frozen picture, and taste
axes in their words), each a small model over on-device encoders. You use it to catch what they would catch before
they see it, and you help them teach it. Every command is in [reference/cli.md](reference/cli.md) under
`raea fingerprint`; the long version is raea.io/docs/fingerprint.

Each step says where it runs, as in SKILL.md: **HEADLESS** (the CLI alone), **PAGE** (their feed open), **PERSON**
(only they can do it).

## What it reads

Every axis reads one sense, on this Mac: pictures through SigLIP 2, sound through CLAP and YAMNet, motion from the
frames, and text (scripts, briefs) through EmbeddingGemma 2. Each axis judges a two-second moment, so a file is judged
only on the senses it has, and a whole piece's story or pace isn't judged at all. Picture axes can learn where in the
frame; sound axes judge the whole sound in each moment. raea has no shipped axis for whether a sound is recorded or
generated: never tell the person the fingerprint says a sound is real, or AI-made.

## Before you post a cut — HEADLESS

```sh
raea fingerprint which out/cut.mp4                 # which fingerprint judges this piece, and why
raea fingerprint score out/cut.mp4                 # the moments it expects a note on, first
raea fingerprint score out/v2.mp4 --was out/v1.mp4 # after a fix: each of v1's flags fixed, still there, or disguised
```

- Score every cut before `feed_post` or `raea show`. Fix each moment that holds it back, or tell the person why you
  didn't. Tell them the axis and the moment in their words, never a number.
- A moment on a picture axis may say where in the frame and, on a render with a layer pass (`--layers`), the layers
  there ("top right on Floor"): start the fix with that layer. `--sheet out.png` boxes it on the frames;
  `--timeline` reads the piece second by second.
- After a fix, score it `--was` the cut before. Only **fixed** counts. **Disguised** means the fix hid the defect
  (a sharpen over a blur, a slow zoom over a freeze) instead of removing its cause: fix the cause.
- An axis that **knows** can hold a post back until the person has looked; one that is **learning** only advises.
  `raea fingerprint report` says which is which and what no axis can judge yet (whether a piece works as a whole,
  story and pace across shots). Don't claim the fingerprint passed what it can't judge.
- A script or a brief scores only on axes that read text, and raea's own axes read pictures and sound, so a script
  scores only once the person has added a text axis.
- A 3D shot: render it with `--layers` and `--aov -o out/shot.aov` beside it, run
  `raea fingerprint things out/shot.mp4 --json > things.json`, then `raea check out/shot.mp4 --things things.json`
  for a thing floating or passing through another, the camera lurching mid-move, or an empty frame.
- A question about the picture and sound that nothing measures ("Does the music fight the voice?"): ask clef-omni
  before you open frames. `raea ask out/cut.mp4 "QUESTION"` (or `--set av`, `--set rubric`, `--set defects`; `raea ask
  list` names them) answers in words and a probability, and says what it looked at and what it cost, from the person's
  plan or their own Cloudflare keys. `--dry` spends nothing. A script asks through `raea/ask` (`ask`, `askMany`), a
  pipeline with `raea ask --batch FILE --json --gate`. Answers are advice until a question is calibrated on the
  person's labels (`raea ask verdict`, `raea ask calibrate`); say so when you pass one on.
- `raea fingerprint score out/cut.mp4 --ask flags` has clef-omni look again at just the moments the fingerprint flags
  (`unsure` for the ones it's unsure of), and says beside each whether clef agrees.
- References the person admires: `raea fingerprint profile REFS... --as NAME`, then `score --profile NAME` says which
  measures fall outside their ranges, where, and which way to move.

## The person's rules

Their standing rules are taste files, nearest first: the project's own `taste.ts`, the workspace's house rules
(`taste.ts` at the workspace's root), then their own (`~/.raea/taste/taste.ts`, and `motion.ts`, `games.ts`,
`sound.ts`, `ui.ts` for each kind of work). A rule may say when it applies and what holds it: a check raea measures, a
script in the project, a fingerprint axis, or nothing but an eye. The file's `about` export keeps these (raea reads
only its default export).

- In the app, `rules_read` lists every rule with the fingerprint that judges the project and its axes, and
  `rule_check out/cut.mp4` holds a file to all of them before `feed_post`: measured rules through
  `raea check --taste`, rules linked to an axis through `raea fingerprint score`, a script by running it, and the
  rest by your own look, which you pass as `verdicts`. Say what broke and where. Headless, run
  `raea check FILE --taste taste.ts` and the score yourself, and look at the rest.
- When the person states a preference for all the work from now, add it with `rule_add` (the project's rules, or the
  workspace's): one plain sentence, why, when it applies, and the axis when one guards against it. It waits in
  Fingerprint › Rules, where they keep, reword, move or drop it (PERSON).
- A rule linked to an axis is only as sure as the axis: one that is **learning** only advises. Linking a rule to an
  axis, or teaching the axis from the notes a rule came from, is the person's (Fingerprint › Rules), not yours.

## Reading their notes

- A note on the picture can carry a mark (a pin, a box, a lasso): fix what's inside it.
- A note on the sound can carry a box drawn on the spectrogram. You read it as "Marked on the sound (box, T0 to T1, LO
  to HI)": a span of time and a band of pitch. The note is about that band in that span (a hiss up high, a hum down
  low), not the whole track: fix it there and leave the rest of the sound alone.
- Notes teach the fingerprint that judged the piece. They become evidence only once the person has checked how they
  were read: `raea fingerprint read PROJECT` reads the pinned notes into kinds and axes (HEADLESS);
  `raea fingerprint readings PROJECT --ask 50` puts them to the person in the app (PERSON); once they agree with 45
  kinds and 40 axes in 50, `raea fingerprint learn-notes PROJECT` makes them evidence. A box's band is kept in the
  label.

## Only when the person asks

These change their fingerprints or commit into their folders. Do each when they ask, not on your own:

| They want to... | Run |
|---|---|
| start a fingerprint, or one for a kind of work that builds on theirs | `raea fingerprint new NAME --about "WHAT IT'S FOR" [--extends me]` |
| teach it from their finished renders | `raea fingerprint bootstrap FILES...` (on-device training; the app's Learn from renders does the same) |
| label a moment, approve a piece, or say one version is better | `teach FILE --axis A --at T --bad`, `approve FILE...`, `pair WORSE BETTER --axis A` |
| keep a fingerprint with a project or workspace, so the team judges with it | `raea fingerprint share NAME --in project PATH` then `raea fingerprint use NAME --in project PATH` (`--in workspace` for all its projects). In the app it's the fingerprint chip beside the project's name: Keep with this project, Keep with the workspace (PERSON) |
| see where two people's tastes differ | `raea fingerprint diff A B` |
| move a lesson from a client's fingerprint up into their own | `raea fingerprint move --fp CHILD --axis A` |
| look back on a finished project | `raea fingerprint postmortem PROJECT` (at most ten yes/no questions in the app, PERSON), then `--tally` |

## Its files

A fingerprint's axes are `~/.raea/fingerprints/NAME/fingerprint.ts`, typed by `raea/fingerprint`
([reference/sdk.md](reference/sdk.md)): add, remove or reword an axis there when the person asks, never its evidence.
Which one judges a piece is decided by where it lives: the project's first, then the workspace's, then the person's
own; at each level the one whose `applies` matches the piece's kind, else that level's default.

# Games and interactive

Pieces a person plays: a composition that reads input and keeps state, drawn in 2D or by Bevy in 3D, played live in
the raea app and rendered to video from the same file. The files under `motion/`, `3d/` and `craft/` are copies of
raea's craft guides (`raea guide NAME` prints the same text).

## Which file to open

| You are... | Open |
|---|---|
| a 2D game: `useInput`, `useGameState`, `useGameEvents`, the build order, a scripted run | [motion/games.md](motion/games.md) |
| a 3D game: state, input, many entities, collisions, state machines | [3d/games.md](3d/games.md), after [3d.md](3d.md) |
| physics (bodies, joints) through a Bevy plugin | [3d/plugins.md](3d/plugins.md) |
| what a game has to do for the people playing it | [craft/modes/play.md](craft/modes/play.md) |
| its sound | [sound.md](sound.md) |
| a game made from shipped game assets (models, kits) | [3d/assets.md](3d/assets.md) |
| a Godot project: scripting it from TypeScript, running it headless, recording its frames | [3d/godot.md](3d/godot.md) |

## The verbs

- `raea play EDIT.tsx` (HEADLESS with `--offscreen`): the game live. `--input-script KEYS.json` plays it from a
  script, `--snapshot T FILE` writes a frame at T seconds, `--json FILE` its report (how fast it opened and ran).
- `raea render EDIT.tsx --input I.json` renders a played run to video, the same frames as the play.
- `raea physics bake|goo|part` bakes what `<Physics>` and `<Goo>` need.
- `raea export-game EDIT.tsx -o OUT --target mac-app|mac-cli` makes the game a program of its own: a Mac app or a
  command, to hand to someone who doesn't have raea.

## Checks

A game is done when `raea play --offscreen` runs its scripted input with no error and its snapshots show what the
script did ([motion/games.md](motion/games.md), "Build order"); render-equals-play rules are in
[3d/limits.md](3d/limits.md).

# Animating ## What to do - Animate text and graphics with declared moves, not per-frame maths. Wrap the part in `` and name its entrance: ``. The engine samples it in Rust on every frame, so a render, live play and a seek all agree, and nothing hard-cuts. - Start from the named moves. Their defaults are the timings the approved pieces were measured to use: - `rise`: y 30 px to 0 over 6 frames, out-cubic, fading in over 5; - `pop`: scale 0.6, then 1.08 at frame 4, then 1 at frame 8; - `slam`: scale 1.3, then 0.96 at frame 4, then 1 at frame 8, for a hit; - `slide`: 30 px from a side over 7 frames (a card arriving); - `wipe`: a clip reveal over 8 frames, in-out-cubic; - `fill`: width 0 to 100% over 24 frames, for a bar starting as the number is said; - `tick({ to })`, called with where it ends (`enter="tick"` alone throws): a number counting up over 24 frames, written as the element's text. It's hidden until its `at` and fades in over 2 frames (`fade: 0` shows it at `from` the whole time). `digits: 2` for decimals, `separator: ","` (or `true`) for 12,345, and `prefix: "$"`, `suffix: " pts"` keep the sign and unit in the same text (write a non-breaking space as `" pts"` in braces, `suffix={" pts"}`, never in a plain JSX attribute string); - `strike`: a line drawn 0 to 100% over 8 frames; - `pushIn`: scale 1 to 1.04 across 90 frames, linear, on footage; - `fade`: opacity 0 to 1 over 6 frames. - Tune a move rather than inventing one: `rise({ distance: 40, frames: 10, ease: "out-quint" })`, `pop({ peak: 1.12 })`, `slide({ from: "right", distance: 64 })`. Vary moves by the part's role, because one move everywhere is a lint. - Give anything that leaves an exit: `exit="fade" exitAt={90}`. The exit is the move played backwards, so it leaves the way it came, with the matching in-curve. - For anything the moves don't cover, key it yourself with `track`: `animate={{ backgroundColor: track({ 0: "#fff", 12: "#ffd400" }) }}`. A track takes numbers or colours (CSS variables work), one curve or one per segment, and `{ repeat: "loop" }`. Keyable properties are `opacity`, `x`, `y`, `scale`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotate`, `width`, `height` (with `{ unit: "%" }`), `clipTop`, `clipRight`, `clipBottom`, `clipLeft`, `blur`, `text`, colours and any numeric style. - Curves are names: `out-cubic` (the settling default), `in-out-cubic` (between two resting places), `in-cubic` (leaving), `linear` (constant motion), `curve.bezier(...)`, and `curve.spring({ damping: 15, stiffness: 120 })`, which stretches a spring over its segment so it lands on the next key. - Order several parts with a timeline instead of hand-adding frame offsets: `timeline(sequence(["card", "rise"], parallel(["title", "pop"], ["cta", "fade"])))`, then ``. Use `` for a list; `grid={{ cols: 3, from: "center" }}` spreads it from the middle. - Declare once. Put moves, tracks and plans at module level, or in `useMemo` when they depend on props, never as new objects built inside a component on every frame. - Keep `interpolate` and `spring` for values that aren't style on one element: a sound's volume, a number fed into layout, a value the code branches on. ## Why A hand-written `interpolate` per property invites made-up numbers: a badge sliding 64 px in 8 frames on an invented bezier, a caption chip that switches colour in one frame, a box that changes size because its scale and its content are computed separately. A named move carries a measured timing, its exit mirrors it, and the engine evaluates it from the frame number, so a frame looks the same however you got to it. `at` and `exitAt` count in the frames of the nearest enclosing ``, like `useCurrentFrame()`, not from the parent ``. A counter inside a badge that enters at frame 110 starts at `at={124}`, not `at={14}`, unless the badge is inside its own Sequence. An `` stays in the layout from the start, invisible until its entrance fades it in, so the boxes around it don't jump when it arrives. Use `mount="during"` when it should only take its space while it shows (a list that grows as replies land). Bounce and elastic curves by reflex are on the floor's refuse list. Use them only when the idea is literally bouncy. ## Common mistakes - A counter or chip whose `at` was counted from its parent `` instead of its Sequence: it finished before the part arrived. - `exit` without `exitAt`: it throws. - Tracks built inline in a component on every frame (`animate={{ y: track(...) }}` inside a big list): hoist them. - A curve name that doesn't exist (`"outCubic"`): the engine logs it once and the track doesn't play. Use the kebab-case names above. - An entrance in CSS `@keyframes` instead of a move. CSS animations do run, on the frame clock from their Sequence's start (a `1s linear` grow is exactly half way at frame 15), but they can't land on a word (`at`) or carry a measured timing and its mirrored exit. - `Math.random()` for an offset that should hold (a jittered layout). It's seeded per frame, so every frame draws new values and the parts shake. Seed from the index: `const x = Math.sin(i * 12.9898) * 43758.5453; const r = x - Math.floor(x);`. - The same pop on every part. ## Example: a stat card that lands, counts up and fills its bar, then leaves ```tsx import { AbsoluteFill, Animate, Composition, fill, pop, registerRoot, rise, tick, timeline, sequence, parallel } from "raea"; import { css } from "./styles.gen"; // declared once: the card rises, then the number pops and counts while the bar fills, then the label fades in const plan = timeline(sequence( ["card", rise({ distance: 30, frames: 7 })], parallel(["number", pop()], ["bar", fill({ to: 73, frames: 24 })], { part: "label", move: "fade", offset: 6 }), )); const COUNT = tick({ to: 73, frames: 24 }); export default function Stat({ label = "of tests ship" }: { label?: string }) { return ( % {label}
); } registerRoot(() => ); ```

# Games: useInput, useGameState, useGameEvents

## What to do

- **Draw the game in an `<Arena>`** (`import { Arena, Banner, Hint, Score } from "raea/arena"`). Give it the
  field's own size, `<Arena width={1600} height={900}>`, and position every child in those units (0 to 1600 across, 0
  to 900 down): the Arena scales the field whole into the middle of whatever stage the game plays on, as bench Pong
  scales its court, so it plays the same in any window. Keep the state in field units too. Never mix in the stage's
  pixels or `useVideoConfig` fractions inside it: a part sized in stage pixels stays big on a small stage and covers
  the rest.
- **The words go in the Arena's parts, never placed by hand.** `score={<Score items={[{ label: "you", value: g.you,
  accent: true }, { label: "house", value: g.house }]} />}` is the top band, a cell per item; `banner={g.phase ===
  "serve" ? <Banner text="space to serve" sub="first to 5" /> : null}` is one message at a time over the field's
  middle, on a plate; `hint={<Hint keys={[{ keys: "↑ ↓", does: "move" }]} />}` is the bottom band. Each has a band of
  its own, so no word lands on another or on the score. Draw no other text over the field.
- **A person plays it.** While someone plays, each frame's input has `live: true` and their keys (`ArrowUp`,
  `ArrowDown`, `w`, `s`, ` `) and pointer: move the player's paddle from them, and let the other side be the
  computer. When no key is down nobody is playing, live or in a render: the step plays itself (below). Never gate that
  on `live`: a game played live sits still until someone presses a key.
- **Renders are landscape**: the composition's size is 1920x1080 at 60 fps unless the request says otherwise, never a
  vertical 9:16 unless asked for. `raea render` and `raea check` use it.
- Write the game as a pure function: `step(state, input, frame) => nextState`. `input` is that frame's
  `{keys: string[], pointer?: {x, y, down}}`, and the step returns a new state object, never a changed old one.
- Read the state at the current frame with `useGameState(initial, step)`. It is `initial` at frame 0, and at frame
  `f` it is `step` applied to each earlier frame in order. Draw the frame from that state.
- Read this frame's input with `useInput()` (`{keys: []}` when there is none), for example to light the keys on screen.
- Cue sound from what happens in the game with `useGameEvents(initial, step, isEvent)`. It runs the same fold to
  the end of the composition and returns, in order, every frame at which `isEvent(before, after)` holds. Each frame
  is the first one that shows the new state. Then place one sound per event:
  `{hits.map((f) => <Sequence from={f} layout="none"><Audio src={thump} /></Sequence>)}`.
- Keep a contact as a flag on the state for the frame it happens on (`paddleContact`, `bricksHit`), so that both the
  step and `isEvent` can read it.
- Frames count from the nearest enclosing Sequence, so a game inside `<Sequence from={60}>` starts at its own
  frame 0 and reads input at the matching composition frames.
- Give the game its input as a script that lives in the file: an `InputTimeline` (`{"<frame>": {"keys": [...]}}`)
  that the step falls back to when the Clock has none, so `raea render` plays it the same way every time.
- Theme the field and the Arena's parts from the brand (`--brand-text`, `--brand-accent`, `--brand-background`) like any
  other piece, each with a fallback colour (`var(--brand-accent, #ff5a36)`): a project with no brand defines none, and
  a bare `var()` draws nothing (an agent's table-tennis game's paddles and net were invisible).
- When an entity has modes (idle, run, jump, hurt; patrol, chase; playing, won, game over), write each as a state
  machine: `machine<Ctx, Env>()({ id, initial, states })` from `raea`, guards polled every frame, delays in
  frames, the snapshot kept in the entity at `sm` and stepped inside the step (`stepAll` for one per enemy). The rules
  and an example are in `bevy/games` ("State machines"); they are the same in 2D.
- For many entities, keep them in an ECS world (`createWorld()` from `raea/ecs`). `spawn`, `set`, `query` and
  `system(fn)` build it, and `world.at(frame)` gives the world after frames 0 to frame-1 have run, the same every
  time it is asked for.

## Build order: render early, keep the scripted run simple

A game that never renders is nothing, so build in this order and render at each step:

1. One `edit.tsx` (and components it imports) with the state, the step and the drawing, rendered with `raea render`
   and looked at (`raea render edit.tsx --at A,B -o stills/`) within your first dozen moves, even if it's only the field and the player moving.
2. Then the rules (collisions, the enemies' machines, win and lose), rendering again after each.
3. **The render's play-through is an autopilot inside the step, not a planner.** When a frame has no keys down
   (live or not), let the step steer the player itself: toward the nearest gem or coin, jump when a gap or an
   enemy is close ahead, a fixed key script by frame, or a mix. A few lines. Never write a search, a route planner or
   a second "mirror" copy of the step to plan the run: the playtest's bots search for a winning run already.
4. **Export `playtest`** from edit.tsx for every game: `initial`, `step` (the same fold), `actions` (the key chords
   a player uses, `[]` included), `observe` (the player's position and what's near, in the units the state keeps),
   `progress` (0 to 1 toward the goal: gems taken over gems needed, distance to the flag over the level's length),
   `outcome` ("won", "lost" or null) and `machines` when it has state machines. A bot then checks the game can be
   won, softlocks nowhere, and reaches every machine state. The import is type-only:
   `import type { Playtest } from "raea"`.
5. **State machines are `machine()` from `raea`**, in 2D as in 3D: read `raea guide bevy/games` ("State
   machines") before writing them. Each entity keeps its snapshot at `sm`, the step calls `m.step(entity, env)`, and
   the playtest's `machines` is `(s) => ({ player: playerM.watch(s.player), ... })`. Your own transition tables or a
   hand-made `{ state, states }` aren't machines to the playtest: its machine checks fail and say so.

## Why

A video frame is a function of its number. `useGameState` folds from the start on every frame, so any frame renders
on its own and the same input always plays the same game, which is what makes a game renderable, checkable and
re-renderable. The fold reuses `initial` each time, so a step that mutates its state corrupts every later frame.

Sound cued from events lands on the frame the thing happens and stays right when the rules change. The approved
Breakout's 31 sounds come from `useGameEvents`, on the same frames that were once placed by hand from a play log.

## Common mistakes

- Mutating the state in `step` (`s.ball.x += s.ball.vx; return s`). Return new objects.
- `Math.random()` in what draws rather than in `step`: it's new every frame, so the thing jumps. In `step` it's seeded
  for that step's frame and repeats on every render and replay; keep what it decides in the state.
- `useState` or `useEffect` to hold the game. Nothing persists between frames; the fold is the state.
- Hand-placing sound frames. Use `useGameEvents`.
- An `isEvent` that holds for several frames in a row (a ball touching the paddle for 3 frames), so one hit gives
  three sounds. Test for the change: `after.contact && !before.contact`.
- A game with no input script, so it sits idle.
- A heavy `step`. It runs about `frame` times per rendered frame, so keep it to arithmetic on plain objects.

## Example: a catch game in an Arena, with input, a score and a sound per point

```tsx
import { Audio, Composition, Sequence, registerRoot, sao, useGameEvents, useGameState, type FrameInput } from "raea";
import { Arena, Banner, Hint, Score } from "raea/arena";
import { css } from "./styles.gen";

// the field's own units: every position below is in these, and the Arena scales them to the stage
const FW = 1600, FH = 900;
const CHIME = sao("bright short arcade coin chime, dry", { seconds: 0.5 });

interface Game { x: number; drop: { x: number; y: number }; score: number; caught: boolean }
const INITIAL: Game = { x: 800, drop: { x: 400, y: 0 }, score: 0, caught: false };

/** One frame of the rules: move the tray, let the drop fall, catch or respawn it. Pure: returns a new state. */
function step(s: Game, input: FrameInput, frame: number): Game {
  const held = (k: string) => input.keys.includes(k);
  // nobody playing: the tray follows the drop by itself, so the stage is never idle
  const dx = input.keys.length ? (held("ArrowRight") ? 16 : 0) - (held("ArrowLeft") ? 16 : 0) : Math.sign(s.drop.x - s.x) * 12;
  const x = Math.min(FW - 120, Math.max(120, s.x + dx));
  const y = s.drop.y + 9;
  const caught = y >= 780 && y < 789 && Math.abs(s.drop.x - x) < 140;
  const respawn = caught || y > FH;
  const nextX = 160 + ((frame * 389) % (FW - 320)); // a seeded column, the same every render
  return { x, drop: respawn ? { x: nextX, y: 0 } : { x: s.drop.x, y }, score: s.score + (caught ? 1 : 0), caught };
}

const isPoint = (before: Game, after: Game) => after.score > before.score;

export default function Catch() {
  const g = useGameState(INITIAL, step);
  const points = useGameEvents(INITIAL, step, isPoint);
  return (
    <Arena width={FW} height={FH}
      score={<Score items={[{ label: "caught", value: g.score, accent: true }]} />}
      banner={g.score === 0 && g.drop.y < 300 ? <Banner text="catch the drops" /> : null}
      hint={<Hint keys={[{ keys: "← →", does: "move the tray" }]} />}>
      <style>{css}</style>
      <div style={{ position: "absolute", left: 0, top: 0, width: FW, height: FH, borderRadius: 24, backgroundColor: "var(--brand-surface, #1b1d24)" }} />
      <div style={{ position: "absolute", left: g.drop.x - 30, top: g.drop.y, width: 60, height: 60, borderRadius: 30, backgroundColor: "var(--brand-accent, #ff5a36)" }} />
      <div style={{ position: "absolute", left: g.x - 120, top: 790, width: 240, height: 36, borderRadius: 18, backgroundColor: "var(--brand-text, #f4efe6)", transform: `scale(${g.caught ? 1.08 : 1})` }} />
      {points.map((p) => (
        <Sequence key={p} from={p} name={`point ${p}`} layout="none">
          <Audio src={CHIME} gainDb={-6} />
        </Sequence>
      ))}
    </Arena>
  );
}

registerRoot(() => <Composition id="catch" component={Catch} width={1920} height={1080} fps={60} durationInFrames={3600} />);
```
