# Parts: a talking take, dressed by name

The reel's parts are designed parts for a talking take. They're an example the project owns: `raea component add reel`
copies them into components/reel/, yours to change, and you import them from "./components/reel". You place each one
with one line, and each one lands on the words that say it. You don't lay out boxes or count frames. You choose which
part goes on which beat, and what it says.

A whole file: the parts go inside `<Ad>` in the piece's component, and `registerRoot` takes a function that returns the
`<Composition>`, which names that component. Never put `<Ad>` inside `<Composition>`: a Composition doesn't render its
children, so nothing would show and nothing would be heard.

```tsx
import { take, bed, SEGMENTS, FACE, FRAMES } from "./take.gen";
import { Composition, Mix, registerRoot } from "raea";
import { Ad, Bed, Captions, Follow, Hook, StatCard, Strike, Take } from "./components/reel";

function Piece() {
  return (
    <Ad>
      <Take src={take} segments={SEGMENTS} face={FACE} />
      <Hook say="nine in ten" text="*9 in 10* / buyers / read reviews first" />
      <StatCard say="only a third" big="33%" text="of shops / answer / *within a day*"
        bars={[{ label: "answer in a day", value: "33%", fill: 0.33 }, { label: "buyers who wait", value: "~10%", fill: 0.1, say: "wait" }]} />
      <Strike say="what works is" text="what works / *a fast reply*" not="not another / discount code" strikeSay="discount code" />
      <Follow say="be sure" text="+ follow for more" />
      <Captions keys="reviews, reply" />
      {bed ? <Bed src={bed} /> : null}
      <Mix lufs={-14} />
    </Ad>
  );
}

registerRoot(() => <Composition id="reviews-reel" component={Piece} width={1080} height={1920} fps={30} durationInFrames={FRAMES} />);
```

## Cues: every part has them

- `say`: the phrase the part lands on, **word for word from the transcript** (case and punctuation don't matter). Two or three words that are said only once. If the phrase is never said, the render stops and names the part. Every part in the band but Phrases gets one (or `beat`): without it a part starts at the piece's first frame, not at its line. Phrases starts on its first phrase by itself.
- `until`: the phrase it leaves on, at the end of that phrase's last word. Without it, the part runs its own length, or until the next part in the top band starts.
- `seconds`: its length, when there's no `until`.
- `occurrence`: which time `say` is said, when a phrase repeats.
- `place`: where it sits. `"top"` (over the head, the default), `"upper"` (lower, over the forehead) or `"middle"` (over the face: for a line that should take the whole picture). Captions keep out of its way wherever it sits. Use it to answer a note about a part's position.
- `sound`: foley on its moment. Each part has its own by default, so leave this alone, or write an SAO prompt, or `false` for none.

## Footage with no voice: cue on the beats

A screen recording or b-roll has no words to cue on, so it's cut on its music: the person's own track (the host's
`bed`), never a pad made to fill the silence. The host cuts the shots on the track's beats and gives `BEATS` (each beat's frame in the cut) and `SHOTS` (where each shot looks). Pass `<Ad beats={BEATS}>`,
and cue each part by beat:

- `beat`: the beat it lands on, counted from 0. A part on a shot's first beat lands on its cut.
- `untilBeat`: the last beat it's up for; it leaves as the next beat starts. A part stays up at least 1.5 s (a bar at most tempos), or the render stops and says which part. Without it, the part runs its own length, or until the next part in the band.

```tsx
import { take, bed, SEGMENTS, SHOTS, BEATS, TONE, FRAMES } from "./take.gen";
import { Composition, Mix, registerRoot } from "raea";
import { Ad, Bed, Callout, EndCard, Hook, Take } from "./components/reel";

function Promo() {
  return (
    <Ad beats={BEATS} tone={TONE} accent="#ff7a1a">
      <Take src={take} segments={SEGMENTS} shots={SHOTS} gain={-20} />
      <Hook beat={0} untilBeat={7} text="plan the week / *in a minute*" />
      <Callout beat={8} untilBeat={15} label="1/3" title="Pick your days" place="middle" />
      <EndCard beat={40} name="Weekly" line="Your week, sorted." cta="weekly.app" />
      {bed ? <Bed src={bed} gain={-15} /> : null}
      <Mix lufs={-14} />
    </Ad>
  );
}

registerRoot(() => <Composition id="weekly-promo" component={Promo} width={1080} height={1920} fps={30} durationInFrames={FRAMES} />);
```

Pass `tone={TONE}` too: on a bright screen the host says "light", and type over the footage turns dark with no grade under it. A card or callout stays up at least a bar so it can be read. Leave out `<Captions>`: nothing is said. The sound is done here too: with `beats`, the parts make a screen piece's foley (a thud on a landing and on each quick cut, a pop on each card), louder than under a voice. Part text comes from the footage's own words, shortened. A screen recording has its own headline at the top, so a card or callout over it goes at `place="middle"`, or the shot zooms in on its subject (`SHOTS` comes from your picks) so the headline is out of the frame.

## The parts

| Part | Props | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `<Take src segments face punch gain>` | `segments`: the kept stretches in the take's seconds, `[[from, to], ...]`; `face`: `{x, y}` shares | the footage, first inside `<Ad>`. The host gives you `segments` and `face`; use them as given |
| `<Hook text>` | `text`: two or three lines, `" / "` between them; a line wrapped whole in `*stars*` is the accent line and pops | the opening line (and a short line worth shouting before the thesis, never the thesis itself) |
| `<StatCard big text bars>` | `big`: the number (`"2%"`); `text`: up to three short lines; `bars`: up to two `{label, value, fill (0..1), say}` | a number the speaker **says**, never one you make up |
| `<Strike text not strikeSay>` | `text`: what's right; `not`: what's wrong, on a card, at most two lines; `strikeSay`: the phrase the strike lands on | "not this, but that" once the thesis is up: the wrong way, named, struck. The thesis's own "not X, but Y" is Phrases |
| `<Phrases text>` | `text`: short phrases the speaker says in turn (it starts where its first phrase is said, so it needs no `say`), `" / "` between them, each word for word (two or three words, as said in one breath); `*word*` accents; it holds until the next part in the band, or give `until` the last phrase's words when the band should empty after it | the thesis, said phrase by phrase: each phrase big on its own, landing on its words and held until the next |
| `<Callout label title detail>` | short words | a step, a claim, a name |
| `<Follow text>` | `"+ follow for more"`: one line; it sits on the accent, so it takes no stars | the ask, when the speaker asks |
| `<EndCard name line cta logo>` | | a brand's close over the whole frame |
| `<Captions keys fix>` | `keys`: words that stay lit once said; `fix`: `"heard=shown"` pairs | always, once, inside `<Ad>` |
| `<Bed src gain>` | | the music under the voice (the host gives `src`) |

`*word*` lights a word in the accent inside any text. Keep lines short: a hook line has two to four words, and a card
line has one to three.

## How a piece reads

- **One part per beat.** The top band (above the face) holds one part at a time. A part ends where the next one starts, so don't stack two on the same words.
- **Open with a Hook** on the first line said. End with the ask (Follow) or an EndCard if there is one. The last one holds to the end of the piece by itself (give it no `until` or `seconds`), so the piece ends on the ask, not on a caption.
- **The parts echo the voice.** A part's words are the speaker's words, shortened. They never contradict the speaker or add a claim.
- **Captions are always on.** They move under a card, hide under a hook, a strike or the ask, and go big at the top when the band is empty. Leave some beats empty so the face and the captions carry them.
- **The thesis gets Phrases.** The thesis is the first line where the speaker says what the brief's `believe:` line means (the believe line finds it; its own wording never goes on screen): the line the piece is about, often the turn after the numbers, and often said as "not this, but that" ("so the fix isn't / another *discount* / it's a *fast reply*"). It reads phrase by phrase: one `<Phrases>` over it, a phrase per breath, the word that carries each phrase in the accent. Captions alone show it three words at a time, lit word by word, which reads as a caption, not a statement.
- **About one part every three to five seconds.** A beat with nothing to show stays empty.
- The sound is done for you. Each part brings its own hit, and `<Mix lufs={-14} />` finishes it, with `<Bed>` when the person gave a track (their own track, or none: never a pad made to fill it). Don't add more foley.

# Sound: Audio, sao and Speech, the music bus, gains, fades, Mix

## What to do

- Decide what each scene is heard as before placing anything: silence, the scene's own sound (footsteps, a room, a
  machine: what the people on screen would hear), source music, score, effects, a voice. Music is a decision per
  scene, never a bed by default (`motion/music` has the spotting and the writing; `motion/sources` where each sound
  can come from).
- Put each sound in its own `<Sequence from={frame} layout="none" name>` with an `<Audio>` inside. The Sequence's
  `from` is when the sound starts, and its `durationInFrames` (optional) cuts it off. `layout="none"` because a sound
  draws nothing.
- Set levels in decibels with `gainDb`. `volume` is the same thing as a linear gain (1 is unity, 0.5 is about -6 dB,
  values above 1 boost). Either one can be a function of the sound's own frame (0 at its first frame) for a duck or
  a swell. `gainDb` wins when both are given.
- Fade with `fadeIn` and `fadeOut`, in seconds. They ramp from and to silence at the start and end of where the sound
  plays, at the audio's own rate, and multiply with the gain. Use about 1 to 1.4 s where an ambience or a source cue
  leaves the scene, and 0.012 s at a cut. A score ends on its last hit instead (`motion/music`).
- Make foley and sound effects with `sao(prompt, {seconds})` (2 s by default; up to 11.9 s, and a longer ask comes
  back 11.9 s long) and pass the result to `<Audio src>`, or take a recorded one from a pack (`motion/sources`).
  Write prompts the way the approved pieces do: the sound, its character and what to leave out ("deep punchy
  cinematic impact hit, tight, no reverb tail"; "bubbly UI pop click, short, dry"). Ask for the length you need.
- Design an effect in layers, each its own short prompt or take, laid on the same frame: a transient (the first 5 to
  30 ms: a snap, a click), a body that says what the thing is (50 to 500 ms), weight for a big hit only (under
  120 Hz, short), and a tail that puts it in its room (0.3 to 3 s). Vary a sound that repeats: 3 to 5 takes (another seed or another file), a semitone or two and a couple of dB apart.
- Give a place its room tone and keep it across that place's cuts: no digital silence under picture, an ambience
  that changes when the place does, and the next scene's sound starting about half a second before its cut. Foley
  is three passes, each on the frame of contact: steps, cloth, props.
- Place what's in the scene where it is: pan it to its side of the frame (`Tone.Panner`, a Channel's `pan`), give
  it the room's reverb, and narrow a device (a phone, a radio) with a high-pass and a low-pass. In 3D, `<Sound3D
  src at>` places it and the camera hears it move.
- When the piece has music, write it in Tone.js on `Tone.buses.music` (`motion/music`): instruments in a `Sampler`
  (a sample library's notes, or TokenSynth's), parts in a `Part` or `Sequence`, composed for the cut. Duck it under
  the voice with `Tone.buses.music.duck(Tone.buses.voice, { amount: -12 })`, give the voice `<Audio bus="voice">`,
  and set the music's level on the bus: `Tone.buses.music.volume.value = -21`, then
  `Tone.buses.music.volume.rampTo(-12, 0.3, t)` to lift it at `t` seconds for the end card.
- Narration over the picture, when the footage has no voice for it, is
  `<Speech text="the words" start={frame} />` from `raea/speech` (Pocket TTS, on this computer; `voice` picks a
  Pocket voice or a WAV of one).
- raea mixes and masters every render: each line of dialogue (the `voice` bus, or footage on no bus) comes to the same
  loudness, a join into dead silence gets the room's tone, and the whole mix comes to -14 LUFS integrated with true
  peaks under -1 dBTP, which is what the floor's loudness defect asks for. Don't level lines with `gainDb` or master
  the voice outside raea. One `<Mix lufs={…} ceiling={…} />` per composition sets another target.
- Put the sounds in the tree in time order. The engine keys a sound's stretch by its place in the tree, so adding a
  sound in the middle of the list can split the ones after it.
- Balance relative to the voice. The approved pieces, mastered to -14 LUFS, sit like this (each a `gainDb` on top of
  raea's level for the voice, or on the sound's own level for the rest):

  | sound | with a voice | without one (promo, deck, game) |
  |---|---|---|
  | the voice clips | about 0 dB | none |
  | music | -21 dB, rising to about -12 dB once the voice stops (the end card) | -12 to -15 dB |
  | foley hits, whooshes, pops | -16 to -22 dB | -1 to -6 dB |

  These are starting points; listen and decide.
- `raea sao "PROMPT" --seconds 1.2 --dir EDIT_DIR -o EDIT_DIR/media/sfx/hit.wav` makes a sound now, to check it
  before it goes in, and keeps it in the edit's asset store (`--dir` is the edit's folder; without it, the folder you
  run it from), so the edit's `sao("PROMPT", { seconds: 1.2 })` then plays that one rather than making another.
  `--seed 2` makes another take of the same prompt; play that file by its path (`staticFile("sfx/hit-2.wav")`), since
  `sao()` has no seed.

## Why

A sound placed without a Sequence starts at frame 0 with everything else. A Sequence with the default layout adds a
full-frame box that paints over the parts beneath it.

`sao()` returns an asset `{kind, prompt, seconds, id, src}` whose id is a stable hash of the kind, the
prompt and the length. The renderer makes each asset once and caches it in the object's `assets/`. SAO runs on this
computer (Stable Audio Open Small, a few seconds a sound; it installs itself the first time, and `motion/sources`
says what that fetches). It does better on effects and field recordings than on music. The same call always reuses
the same sound, and changing one word of the prompt makes a new one. So settle the prompt before you iterate on
gains.

Policy: music is notes on Tone.js instruments (sample libraries first, TokenSynth, synths), SAO and recorded packs
make effects and foley, and Pocket TTS (`<Speech>`) says narration over the picture, all on this computer. Any other
generation is a `raea gen` step (`motion/gen`). (`lyria()`, a remote music model, is retired: a new take is refused,
and music written as notes can be cut on the bar and edited note by note anyway.)

Sound sells the cut, but one move everywhere is a lint: a whoosh on every entrance flattens all of them. Give
foley to the moments that are physical (a slam, a strike-through, a card landing on the beat) and let others be
silent.

## Check the sound before you call it done

Frames get looked at; sound has to be measured, because a broken mix is easy to miss on one listen and obvious to
everyone else. Two checks, both cheap:

- **The render says when a sound runs out.** `WARN  sound X runs out N s before its stretch ends` means the
  source is shorter than its Sequence and still sounding (or asked for a fadeOut) at its end: it stops dead and the
  fade never plays, so a 10 s `sao()` ambience under a 12 s scene cuts off mid-line. `loop` alone doesn't help: a
  sound loops only between `startFrom` and `endAt`, and that loop is a hard jump. Tile it instead: copies of the take
  end to end, each in its own Sequence, crossfading over 1.5 s (`fadeIn`/`fadeOut`), or make the take as long as the
  span.
- **Check the finished file.** `raea check FILM.mp4 --words words.json` (the voice's words on the film's clock)
  reports, by timecode, dead stops (a steady sound that ends in one 10 ms step: fade it out over 100 ms or more;
  a voice ending its word isn't one), stretches with no voice louder than
  the voice, music closer than 12 dB to the voice over it, and a true peak over -1 dBTP. Fix every line it prints, or
  say why it stands.

Set levels from measurements, not by ear on one pass. Measure each source's integrated loudness (`ffmpeg -i F -af
ebur128 -f null -`) and set its gain against the narration's: music 15-20 LU under the voice; a film's own sound,
where the narration stops, about 3 LU under it with its loudest 3 s no more than 2 LU over; never boost a near-silent
take more than +3 dB (its hiss comes up with it). A flat gain on every archive clip is how one film's main title
ends up shouting over the narrator while another is inaudible.

## Common mistakes

- An `<Audio>` without a Sequence, or in a Sequence without `layout="none"`.
- `volume={-6}` meaning decibels. That throws, because volume is a non-negative linear gain. Write `gainDb={-6}`.
- Music at -6 dB under the voice. The voice must stay intelligible over everything (floor).
- A pad, a drone or one `sao()` take of "ambient music" laid under the whole piece as its score. Decide what each
  scene needs, and write the music (`motion/music`).
- An effect from one take with nothing under it: a click that should be a door. Layer it.
- `loop` on an `<Audio>` without `endAt` to stretch a short ambience: nothing loops, it plays once and stops dead
  (the render warns). With `endAt` it repeats with a hard jump at each loop; tile copies with crossfades instead.
- Two `<Mix>` in one composition: it throws.
- Rewording a `sao()` prompt on every pass. Each new prompt makes a new sound.
- `style` on an `<Audio>`: Audio has no picture and takes no style.
- Hand-placing dozens of game sounds from a log. Cue them from `useGameEvents` (`motion/games`).
- Writing music note by note in `<Audio>` files, or a game's sounds by hand. Write them in Tone.js (`motion/music`):
  instruments, the Transport, buses with ducking, and `<Tone.Sfx>` for one-shots.

## Example: a cue that lands on the end card, a voice, a layered hit

```tsx
import { AbsoluteFill, Audio, Composition, Mix, Sequence, registerRoot, sao, staticFile } from "raea";
import * as Tone from "raea/tone";
import { css } from "./styles.gen";

const FRAMES = 300;
const END_CARD = 252; // the voice stops here

// the music (motion/music): a sampled piano, chords that change every bar under a motif that answers the voice,
// ducked under it, lifted for the end card, and ending on a chord on that cut. The tempo is set from the cut:
// four bars to the end card, so its cut is a downbeat.
Tone.getTransport().bpm.value = (4 * 4 * 60 * 30) / END_CARD; // about 114 bpm
Tone.buses.music.duck(Tone.buses.voice, { amount: -12 });
Tone.buses.music.volume.value = -21;
Tone.buses.music.volume.rampTo(-12, 0.33, END_CARD / 30);
// `raea sounds get salamander/piano` printed its roots a minor third apart (D#2 is the file Ds2.mp3); these cover
// F2 to G5, what the cue plays
const ROOTS = ["D#2", "F#2", "A2", "C3", "D#3", "F#3", "A3", "C4", "D#4", "F#4", "A4", "C5", "D#5", "F#5"];
const piano = new Tone.Sampler({
  urls: Object.fromEntries(ROOTS.map((n) => [n, staticFile(`sounds/salamander-piano/${n.replace("#", "s")}.mp3`)])),
  release: 1,
}).connect(new Tone.Reverb({ decay: 1.4, wet: 0.2 }).connect(Tone.buses.music));
const CHORDS = [["A2", "E3", "C4"], ["F2", "C3", "A3"], ["C3", "G3", "E4"], ["G2", "D3", "B3"]];
new Tone.Part((t, c) => piano.triggerAttackRelease(c.notes, "4n", t, c.vel), CHORDS.flatMap((chord, bar) => [
  { time: `${bar}:0`, notes: chord, vel: 0.55 },
  { time: `${bar}:2:2`, notes: chord, vel: 0.4 },
])).start(0);
new Tone.Part((t, n) => piano.triggerAttackRelease(n.note, "8n", t, n.vel), [
  { time: "1:1", note: "E5", vel: 0.7 }, { time: "1:1:2", note: "D5", vel: 0.5 }, { time: "1:2", note: "C5", vel: 0.6 }, { time: "1:3", note: "A4", vel: 0.65 },
  { time: "3:1", note: "G5", vel: 0.75 }, { time: "3:1:2", note: "F5", vel: 0.5 }, { time: "3:2", note: "E5", vel: 0.6 }, { time: "3:3", note: "D5", vel: 0.7 },
]).start(0);
Tone.getTransport().schedule((t) => piano.triggerAttackRelease(["A2", "E3", "A3", "C4", "E4"], "1m", t, 0.8), "4m");
Tone.getTransport().start();

// one hit in three layers, on the same frame: the snap that starts it, the body that says what it is, the room's tail
const SNAP = sao("sharp wooden snap, close, very short, dry", { seconds: 0.3 });
const HIT = sao("deep punchy impact hit, tight, no reverb tail", { seconds: 1.2 });
const TAIL = sao("the reverb tail of one impact in a large hall, no attack", { seconds: 2.5 });
const POP = sao("bubbly UI pop click, short, dry", { seconds: 0.6 });
const VOICE = staticFile("voice/vo01.wav"); // the person's narration, as a file

/** Every sound, in time order. */
const SOUNDS = [
  { id: "hit-snap", from: 0, gainDb: -20, src: SNAP, fade: 0, bus: "sfx" },
  { id: "hit", from: 0, gainDb: -16, src: HIT, fade: 0, bus: "sfx" },
  { id: "hit-tail", from: 0, gainDb: -24, src: TAIL, fade: 0, bus: "sfx" },
  { id: "voice", from: 15, to: END_CARD, gainDb: 0, src: VOICE, fade: 0.012, bus: "voice" },
  { id: "pop", from: END_CARD + 2, gainDb: -17, src: POP, fade: 0, bus: "sfx" },
] as const;

export default function SoundBed() {
  return (
    <AbsoluteFill style={{ backgroundColor: "var(--brand-background)" }}>
      <style>{css}</style>
      {SOUNDS.map((s) => (
        <Sequence key={s.id} from={s.from} durationInFrames={"to" in s ? s.to - s.from : undefined} name={s.id} layout="none">
          <Audio name={s.id} src={s.src} gainDb={s.gainDb} fadeIn={s.fade} fadeOut={s.fade} bus={s.bus} />
        </Sequence>
      ))}
      <Mix lufs={-14} ceiling={-1.5} />
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
}

registerRoot(() => <Composition id="sound" component={SoundBed} width={1080} height={1920} fps={30} durationInFrames={FRAMES} />);
```

# Planning and tasks: the project's plan.org

Every raea project keeps its work in one file, `plan.org` at the top of its folder. It is plain Org mode text (Emacs's
outline format), and it is the to-do list the person sees in the raea app. It is the only list: the brief says what
to make and holds no tasks, and a message from the person isn't a task until you plan one. You keep it: plan in it
before work of more than one step, put on each task the feed item it waits on, close it with what you made, and add
what you find left to do. Do this whether or not the person ever opens it; a plan nobody maintains is a blank list,
and a blank list tells them nothing about where their project stands.

An object's build plan (the parts a procedural object is checked against) is `NAME.parts.ts`, not this.

## Where it is, and how you reach it

- In the raea app (it launched you): the plan tools, `plan_read`, `plan_add`, `plan_update` and `plan_close`
  ([reference/feed.md](reference/feed.md)). Each turn's prompt also carries `raea://plan/<project>`: the open tasks by
  id. Use the tools rather than writing the file yourself, so the person's list changes at once.
- Anywhere else (a terminal in the project's folder, a headless run): open `plan.org` and edit it as text. Keep every
  `:ID:` as it is, and give a new task one (`t-` and eight lowercase letters and digits; the app gives one to a task
  that has none the next time an agent reads the plan). The app reads the file again while the person's to-do list is
  open and before each of its agents' turns, so they see your changes. With no `plan.org` yet, start one with the head
  below.
- Find the folder with `raea project --json` (SKILL.md section 0). The plan sits beside `brief.ts` or `brief.md`.

## What a plan looks like

```org
#+TITLE: Stay
#+TODO: TODO | DONE DROPPED

* Look
** TODO [#A] Light the oil door [1/3]                                      :look:
DEADLINE: <2026-11-20 Fri>
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       t-k3x9q2ab
:AGENT:    a-light
:ITEM:     i-door-2
:END:
- [X] warm key from the lamp
- [ ] cool fill from the window
- [ ] rim on the handle
** DONE Grade the hall
CLOSED: [2026-11-14 Sat 16:40]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       t-k3x8m1zz
:ITEM:     i-hall-2
:END:
Graded warm; the window stays cold. [[item:i-hall-2]]
* Sound
** TODO Score the door opening
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       t-k3xa0c4d
:END:
```

- **Headings without a keyword are stages** (`* Look`, `* Sound`): they group the tasks under them. A task is a
  heading with a keyword.
- **Keywords are the file's own.** The `#+TODO:` line lists them, and its `|` splits the open words from the ones that
  close a task. A plan the app makes has `TODO | DONE DROPPED`: `TODO` open, `DONE` finished, `DROPPED` no longer
  wanted. A team's plan may have more (`TODO MAKING REVIEW | DONE DROPPED`, or its own words on another `#+TODO:`
  line); raea reads any of them that way. Use the plan's own words and add none of yours. Where an open task stands
  (under way, waiting on the person) is read from its item and from the work on it, so you needn't mark it as you go.
- **Priority** `[#A]`, `[#B]` or `[#C]`, after the keyword. Use A for what blocks everything else, sparingly.
- **Tags** after the words, between colons: `:look:sound:`. Letters, digits and `_`: write a dash as `_`
  (`act_one`). A task inherits its stage's tags. The feed's views and an item's tags read them.
- **Dates** on one line right after the heading, the planning line: `DEADLINE: <2026-11-20 Fri>` when it's due,
  `SCHEDULED:` when to start it, and `CLOSED: [...]`, stamped when a task closes (in the app the tools stamp it). All
  three share that one line; Org reads no second planning line, and a drawer under one is lost to it.
- **Properties**, in the drawer: `:ID:` (every task has one, and it never changes), `:ITEM:` the feed item it stands
  on or made, `:AGENT:` who has it by agent id (an `@name` while no agent has that name), `:FROM:` what asked for it
  (`ITEM#COMMENT` for each note it answers, separated by spaces), `:LINK:` the same task in another tracker (below).
  Anything else you add is kept.
- **Links** by id, never by title: `[[item:i-hall-2]]` for a feed item, `[[id:t-k3x9q2ab]]` for another task.

## When to plan

Planning is part of the work, not a step you may skip: the plan is how the person sees what you're doing, and the
list they act on. Plan before you make anything that takes more than one step, and keep the plan true as you go.

- **Before work of more than one step**: write its steps as tasks under a stage, each one small enough to finish in
  a turn or two. A one-step ask needs no task: do it and answer.
- **When the person sends you notes** (a round of comments on an item, or a list of fixes in a message): plan them
  before you touch anything. See the next section.
- **At the start of a project**: its stages (Look, Script, Make, Sound, Deliver, or what fits), with the first few
  tasks under each. A long plan nobody will reach is noise: plan the next stretch in detail and the rest as stages.
- **When you find more to do** (a fix a critique asks for, a shot you need, a question for the person): add it where
  it belongs, instead of keeping it in your head or in a chat message.

## Notes from the person: plan them first

A round of notes is what the person saw, in their words ("jaw looks broken", "splats here", "approved! looks
good!"). It isn't a plan, and copied into the to-do list it tells nobody what will be done. So before you change
anything:

1. **Read every note in the round**, with where it's pinned and what's on the item there.
2. **Write the work as tasks, in your words**: what you'll change, where, and what done looks like. "Rebuild the jaw
   hinge so the mouth opens without tearing at the corners", not "jaw looks broken". Several notes that are one fix
   are one task (its steps as checkboxes); one note that is several fixes is several tasks.
3. **Link each task to the notes it answers**: `:FROM:` the item and comment ids as `ITEM#COMMENT`, as many as it
   answers, separated by spaces (`:FROM: i-head-5#c-a1 i-head-5#c-a4`). In the app that's `plan_add` with
   `"from": "i-head-5#c-a1 i-head-5#c-a4"`. The person's to-do list then shows your tasks in place of their notes;
   a note no task names stays listed as waiting for you.
4. **A note that asks for nothing** (an approval, a thank-you, a question you answer in a line) gets no task: settle
   it at once (`comment_task` with `state: "done"` and a line; outside the app `raea show --on ITEM --done ID --note
   LINE`).
5. **Then work the tasks in order**: mark the notes each one answers working as you start it (`comment_task`), and
   close both when the version that settles them is posted (`feed_post` with `answers`, or `raea show FILE --replaces
   ITEM --done ID...`).

## As you work

1. **Start**: read the plan (`plan_read`, or the turn's plan block). Find the task you're on, or add it.
2. **As you go**, tick its checkboxes as each step is done (`plan_update` with `check: N`, 0 first).
3. **Waiting on the person** (a pick, an approval, a note): put the item they're to look at on the task (`plan_update`
   with `item`). When they approve that item, or any later version of it, the task closes DONE on its own, stamped
   `CLOSED`, with nobody asked. That's how the storyboard a gate waits on, a cut sent for approval or a question they
   answer closes its task.
4. **Close it** as you finish, in the same turn, when nothing waits on the person: `plan_close` with the item you
   posted (feed_post's answer) and one line on what was done. That stamps `CLOSED` and links the work. Outside the
   app: change the keyword to the plan's closing word (`DONE`), put `CLOSED: [YYYY-MM-DD Day HH:MM]` at the start of
   the planning line (make one right under the heading when it has no DEADLINE or SCHEDULED), and put the item's id
   in `:ITEM:`.
5. **No longer wanted**: `plan_close` with `state: "dropped"` and why. Remove a task only when it was a mistake; a
   dropped task keeps the record of what was decided.
6. **Before you end the turn**: every task you finished is closed, and every one that waits on the person has its
   item on it.

The calls, as the app's tools take them (every task by its id, from `plan_read` or the turn's plan block):

```text
plan_read   {}                                    or {"full": true} for the whole file
plan_add    {"tasks": [{"title": "Light the oil door", "under": "Look", "checks": ["warm key", "cool fill"]},
                       {"title": "Rim on the handle", "under": "t-k3x9q2ab"}]}
plan_add    {"tasks": [{"title": "Rebuild the jaw hinge so the mouth opens without tearing", "under": "Fixes",
                        "from": "i-head-5#c-a1 i-head-5#c-a4", "checks": ["hinge pivot", "corner weights"]}]}
plan_update {"changes": [{"id": "t-k3x9q2ab", "check": 0}]}
plan_update {"changes": [{"id": "t-k3x9q2ab", "item": "i-door-2"}]}    the person approving i-door-2 closes it
plan_close  {"id": "t-k3x9q2ab", "item": "i-door-3", "note": "Warm key at 3200K, cool fill from the window."}
plan_close  {"id": "t-k3xa0c4d", "state": "dropped", "note": "The person cut the scene."}
```

`under` is a stage heading's words (made when there's none) or a task's id (a subtask); an id that isn't in the plan
is refused, not made into a stage. Each answer lists the open tasks again, with the new ids.

## Big work: subtasks, checkboxes and progress

- **Subtasks** for steps that each take real work or go to different agents: `plan_add` with `under:` the parent's id.
  A parent with `[/]` (or `[%]`) in its words gets a cookie that counts its closed subtasks: `[2/5]`, `[40%]`.
- **Checkboxes** for small steps inside one task (`checks` on `plan_add`, `add_check` on `plan_update`): `- [ ]` and
  `- [X]` under the heading. With no subtasks, the cookie counts these.
- Keep it to two levels under a stage where you can. A plan the person can skim beats a complete one.

## What the person sees

The to-do list in the app (the checkbox in a feed's header, and the Inbox's for every project) is this file: one line
a task with its checkbox, its words and who has it; subtasks under their parents; done tasks folded under a count.
They add, tick, reword, reorder and remove tasks there, and those are edits to `plan.org` too, so read the plan before
you change it rather than trusting what you read earlier. A round of notes sent on an item shows as one line ("6
notes on “Head v5”") until you plan it; then your tasks stand in its place. The notes themselves you mark with
`comment_task` ([collaborate.md](collaborate.md)).

## The same task in another tracker: :LINK:

A team that also tracks work in Linear, Asana, Jira, GitHub or its own system keeps a task in step with its item
there. Nothing in raea is written per tracker: the file says it all.

```org
#+TODO: TODO MAKING REVIEW | DONE DROPPED
#+LINK_STATES: linear In Progress=MAKING; In Review=REVIEW; Done=DONE; Canceled=DROPPED

** REVIEW Hero cut
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       t-k3xb7e2q
:LINK:     linear:ENG-12 asana:1209876543
:END:
```

- **`:LINK:`** names the task's item in each other tracker as `SYSTEM:ID`, one per system, separated by spaces. The ID
  is the tracker's own key (`ENG-12`, `acme/site#12`, a Trello short link), never a URL; a URL goes in the task's text.
  One tracker item is one task. Never change a `:LINK:` someone else wrote: a sync reads it.
- **`#+LINK_STATES:`** in the head, one line a system, maps that tracker's statuses to the plan's keywords
  (`Status=KEYWORD`, separated by `;`). A status coming in becomes its keyword; a keyword going out becomes the first
  status listed for it. Each keyword must be one of the plan's `#+TODO:` words.
- **Fix what's wrong yourself.** `checkPlan` (below) names each problem with its fix: an entry that isn't
  `SYSTEM:ID`, a URL, a system twice on one task, one tracker item on two tasks, a mapped keyword the plan doesn't
  have. Nothing else is required, so headings that only group, hold notes or hold settings are never flagged.

## Extending it: @raea/task

`@raea/task` (raea's `sdk/task`) is the plan in TypeScript, and what the app itself uses. A plugin or a script can:

```ts
import { readPlan, applyEdits, openTasks, definePlanKind, defineKeywords, defineProperty, checkPlan, trackersOf, keywordFor, statusFor } from "@raea/task"
import { usePlan, PlanOutline, Agenda, BoardLanes } from "@raea/task/react"

defineKeywords({ name: "shots", words: "SHOT LIT GRADED | APPROVED" })
defineProperty({ key: "SHOT", about: "the shot's number", check: (v) => (/^\d+[a-z]?$/.test(v) ? undefined : "a shot number, like 12 or 12a") })
definePlanKind({ name: "shot", keywords: "shots", props: ["SHOT"], defaults: { tags: ["shot"] } })

const plan = readPlan(text)                       // every heading, every task, nothing lost
const { text: next } = applyEdits(text, [         // edits by id; every line it didn't touch is kept byte for byte
  { op: "add", title: "Shot 12: the door", kind: "shot", props: { SHOT: "12" }, under: "Look" },
  { op: "state", ref: "t-k3x9q2ab", state: "done", item: "i-door-3" },
])
checkPlan(readPlan(next))                         // what's wrong, each with its fix: links, ids, kinds, properties
trackersOf(plan.tasks[0])                         // [{ system: "linear", id: "ENG-12" }]: its :LINK: entries
keywordFor(plan, "linear", "In Review")           // "REVIEW": a status coming in, by #+LINK_STATES:
statusFor(plan, "linear", "DONE")                 // "Done": the status a keyword goes out as
```

A word of a plugin's sequence written into a plan adds that sequence's `#+TODO:` line to the file's head, so Emacs
cycles it too. `applyEdits` keeps every line it didn't change byte for byte; a heading whose keyword changes keeps its
spacing and its tags' column, as Org's own `org-todo` does.

`board`, `agenda` and `outline` are views of a plan; `defineView` adds one, and `useView(plan, name)` builds it in
React. `answerPlanTool` answers the four plan tools on any text, for a host of your own.

# ComputeKit v4.6 — Agent 直接调度（用户指定）
本版取代 v4.5 的中央资源租约和独立 watchdog 方案。**不部署 Compute Gateway、Cloudflare Worker/DO/Workflow/Cron、看门狗或常驻计算代理。** Cloudflare KV 仅可用于既有技能版本分发，与算力调用无关。Agent 自己选择并使用已经合法授权、真实可用的本地/沙盒/CI/Colab 工具；无权限时继续可用研发并记录 PENDING，不假设所有 AI 都能执行。
## 1. 权限和任务准备
每个 Agent 在自身支持的客户端一次性接入官方 Colab CLI 或 MCP（具体依客户端能力和官方授权流程）；只用自己已授权的身份。禁止共享 Google 密码、OAuth token、Cookie 或把凭证写进 GitHub/KV/聊天；不能用技能文件给客户端添加实际工具权限。认证有效性、CLI help/版本、会话列表可用非分配调用检查。读取官方 integrations/colab-operator/SKILL.md，优先本地 CLI 官方 colab run 单次任务；浏览器桥接需对应本地客户端，不能假设任意云 Agent 可用。
提交前定义 revision、输入哈希、seed、能力、正确性 oracle、输出、依赖、时限、费用估计和用户已授权预算；所有代码/测试和上传文件预先准备好。外传数据须获授权，禁止附带密钥。先用本地 CPU 或免费已验证环境，只有需要外部并行/图形能力或真实期限时考虑远程。CUDA 与 WebGPU/图形能力分别检查，云端不代替目标手机验收。已知硬件型号和费率才可自动消耗已授权 CU，不自动购买；未知预算或费率时仅用可确认免费的环境或请用户授权。每个 Agent 单独记录预算，不存在中央原子总账：多 Agent 同账号不能保证全局并发/总费用限制；建议人为给各 Agent 分配独立额度并避免并行启动，不能把本地限制宣传为全局强制。
## 2. 按需启动，执行完即关
默认使用已核验的 colab run -s UNIQUE_NAME [--gpu T4] SCRIPT.py（不加 --keep）；使用已准备好的脚本，集中跑数值验证、回归、图形测试，结果按需回传，正常退出后核实 provider 会话列表。显卡必须用该版本官方 allowlist，未知型号不能默默升级 A100。对 MCP/API：先确认实际工具支持创建、执行、取回结果、真正删除 Runtime 和查询状态；仅停止代码、断开连接或删除 Jupyter session 不等于 VM 释放。若缺少生命周期控制，不自动申请付费算力。
同一不中断的工具调用中可批量执行已准备的多个任务；若自行 new/exec/stop，用 try/finally 清理并校验，记录唯一名称、账户范围、运行时 ID 和所属任务。decideIdle() 只在同一执行批次内部、下一批已准备、保留成本严格小于重启、时限和预算仍足够且 finally 可用时允许短暂 KEEP_IN_BATCH；默认300秒只是同批次的可调保护上限，不是固定等待，也不是实际后台定时器。**一旦要返回模型思考、修改源码、等待用户、跨工具调用或结束任务，立即释放；不跨 Agent 回合保留付费 VM。** 如一次性官方 run 能完成所有任务，不另行手动保留会话。
## 3. 正常清理及风险
执行结束/报错/可处理的取消都在当前工具生命周期中尝试 stop/delete exact owned runtime，再确认 provider 状态。禁止误删用户或其他 Agent 的会话。创建超时先按唯一名称查询，避免重复创建。失败记 CLEANUP_PENDING，停止该 Agent 后续付费申请，能操作时限次重试；恢复会话时先核对自己的历史未关闭任务。无法确认则报告真实运行时 ID/名称及手动终止路径。未确认释放不可宣称不再扣费。
不设 watchdog、定时轮询服务、后台租约清理或 Cloudflare 调度。硬断线、进程被杀、权限失效、provider 故障仍可能留下计费 VM；这是用户选择简化架构后的剩余风险。一次性 colab run 的正常清理不保证 SIGKILL 后必定释放；需用户在 Colab 管理会话中手动回收。不要靠保活规避限制。
## 4. 自主纠错与证据
自动执行最小可复现测试→读取报错/误差/截图→按根因修复→仅复测受影响部分→保留 revision、环境、日志、指标和释放状态。缓存匹配的测试证据，避免重复花费。无需算力时不启动。没有 Colab 工具也不阻塞项目。
tools/compute-policy.mjs 提供 chooseBackend、decideIdle、decideCleanup 三个纯策略函数；不能代替真实 CLI/MCP 操作。模块入口 node tools/module-router.mjs compute；测试 node --test tests/test_compute_policy.mjs。本次没有连接或启动 Colab，无实时账单验证；实际调用权来自客户端的用户授权，不来自技能同步。
files.integrations/colab-operator/SKILL.md:
---
name: colab-operator
description: Operate Google Colab environments via the `colab` CLI. Use when asked to create or manage GPU/TPU sessions, run Python/shell on a remote Colab VM, sync files, automate environment setup (packages, auth, Drive), or export session history.
---

# Skill: Colab Session Operator

Operate Google Colab environments via the `colab` CLI: provision GPU/TPU sessions, run Python/shell on the VM, sync files, and capture work as notebooks.

## Installation

If the user does not already have the `colab` tool installed, it can be acquired
by running `uv tool install google-colab-cli` or `pip install google-colab-cli`.

## When to activate
- Creating or managing TPU/GPU sessions.
- Running Python or shell on a remote Colab VM.
- Syncing files between local and remote.
- Automating environment setup (packages, auth, Drive).
- Exporting session history as a Jupyter notebook.

## Mental model (read this first)
- **A session == a live Jupyter kernel on a rented VM.** `colab new` allocates a billable VM; `colab stop` releases it. Sessions stay alive as long as the kernel is active, with the Colab backend automatically maintaining liveness.
- **Kernel state PERSISTS across `colab exec` / `colab repl` calls in the same session.** Each invocation reattaches to the *same* kernel (the kernel ID is cached in local state) and only closes the websocket on exit — it does **not** shut the kernel down. So imports, variables, and defined functions survive between separate `colab exec` commands. Build up state incrementally; don't re-import everything each call. (`colab stop` and `colab restart-kernel` are what actually reset it.)
- **Default working directory is `/content`.** Every `exec`/`repl`/`run` `cd`s there first; prefer absolute paths (`/content/...`) for file work. For `colab ls/rm/upload/download`, absolute `/content/...` paths work and the default `ls` path is `content` (VM root).
- **`colab` is fire-and-forget.** Each command authenticates, does one thing, and exits.

## Authentication (the #1 thing that blocks agents)
- The global flag is `--auth={oauth2,adc}` and the **default is `oauth2`**. Pass `--auth=adc` *before* the subcommand to use Application Default Credentials: `colab --auth=adc new -s x`.
- **ADC setup** (`--auth=adc`, most reliable for headless/agent use). The Colab backends need a specific scope set, so re-mint ADC with all four scopes:
  ```bash
  gcloud auth application-default login \
      --scopes=openid,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/colaboratory
  ```
  Why all four: `colaboratory` and `userinfo.email` (required by the session backend `colab.research.google.com`, else 401), `openid`+`cloud-platform` (mandated by gcloud itself; it rejects scope lists missing `cloud-platform`).
- **oauth2 setup** (default): `colab <anything>` (or `colab --auth=oauth2 <anything>`) triggers a browser consent flow on first use (token cached in the OS keyring via `keyring`). Requires a client config at `~/.colab-cli-oauth-config.json` (or `-c PATH`), falling back to the bundled config. The browser step means it usually needs a human; prefer `--auth=adc` for agents.
- **Verify auth in one shot**: `colab sessions` (read-only, lists server assignments) or `colab whoami` (hidden debug command: prints the active email, scopes, audience, and expiry). When any call 401s or 403s, the cause is almost always missing credentials or scopes — `colab whoami` shows it instantly.
- **Do NOT confuse `colab auth` with CLI authentication.** `colab auth` injects *VM-side* GCP credentials into the running kernel (so notebook code can call BigQuery/GCS); it is orthogonal to how the CLI itself authenticates. Never suggest "run `colab auth`" to fix a CLI 401/403 — that's a scope/identity problem fixed via the `gcloud` command above.

## Workflow

### Provision
- `colab new -s <name>` (CPU). Add `--gpu A100` or `--tpu v6e1` for accelerators. **Always pass `-s <name>`** — an omitted name is auto-generated as a random 6-hex string, which makes later commands ambiguous.
- Supported `--gpu`: `T4`, `L4`, `G4`, `H100`, `A100`. Supported `--tpu`: `v5e1`, `v6e1`.
- **Gotcha**: an unrecognized `--gpu` value silently falls back to **A100** (which then usually fails the next step). A `400` on `colab new` with an accelerator means no quota/entitlement for it on this account — fall back to `--gpu T4` or omit the flag for CPU.
- Accelerator availability is tier-gated; most accounts can only get CPU. Don't assume a GPU/TPU will allocate.

### Execute
- **Preferred**: `colab exec -s <name> -f <script.py>` runs a local script on the remote VM (read locally, sent to the kernel — no manual upload needed).
- **Piped code**: `echo "print(1)" | colab exec -s <name>` or `cat script.py | colab exec -s <name>`.
- **Notebooks**: `colab exec -s <name> -f nb.ipynb` runs each code cell and writes results to `<basename>_output.ipynb` next to the input. A `# @title Foo` first line labels the cell in progress output.
- **Plots/images**: PNG/JPEG outputs are intercepted. Use `--output-image <path>` on `exec`/`repl` to save to a known location (otherwise a temp path is printed). Inline terminal-image escapes are auto-suppressed when stdout isn't a TTY, so piped/captured output stays clean.
- **Shell**: run a one-shot shell command with `colab ssh -s <name> -- <cmd>`: it runs in `/content` and exits with the command's status. Output is byte-exact when stdout is piped or redirected; ssh allocates a PTY only when stdin and stdout are both terminals, so a shell tool that runs commands in a terminal should add `</dev/null` and redirect the output to a file (a pipe keeps `colab ssh`'s exit status only under `set -o pipefail`). One argument is a shell command line (quote it for pipes or globs: `colab ssh -s <name> -- 'nvidia-smi | head -5'`); several arguments are an exact argv, so pass untrusted values as separate arguments after `--` where the program accepts it (e.g. `colab ssh -s <name> -- ls -- "$f"`), never inside a shell line or a piped script. Pipe a multi-line script to `colab ssh -s <name> -- bash`. Use `colab exec` for Python code. When ssh can't work (no local `ssh` client, no `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` or `id_ecdsa` key and no `-i KEY`, a tool not on the minimal ssh environment's `PATH` such as `gcloud` or `node`, or the runtime's limited concurrent SSH connections in use, which the server answers with 429, e.g. while a person or an IDE is connected), fall back to `exec` with IPython's `!` prefix: `echo '!df -h /content' | colab exec -s <name>` (single quotes stop your local shell expanding `!`). Each `!` line runs in its own shell with no input (a command that prompts hangs), and IPython evaluates `{expr}` as Python even inside quotes and expands `$name` outside single quotes. Start a multi-line script with a `%%bash` line (not with `--env`, which prepends Python lines), use non-interactive flags such as `apt-get -y`, and never put untrusted text in a `%%bash` script or a `!` line (even via `{var}` or `$var`): pass it with `--env NAME=VALUE` and run `subprocess.run(["cmd", "--", os.environ["NAME"]])` from Python. For an interactive shell on the VM, a human runs `colab ssh -s <name>`.
- **Never run `colab repl`, `colab ssh` without `-- CMD`, `colab auth`, or `colab drivemount` interactively from an agent** — `repl`, `auth` and `drivemount` expect a TTY and will hang or fail, and bare `colab ssh` with no saved session creates a billable runtime; an interactive shell is for a human. `repl` accepts piped stdin and exits on EOF; `auth`/`drivemount` genuinely require a human at the terminal.

### Ephemeral one-shot jobs (`colab run`)
- `colab run [--gpu T4] [--tpu v6e1] [--keep] [-s NAME] script.py [args...]` = `new` + `exec` + `stop` in one command. It provisions a fresh VM, runs the script with `sys.argv` and `__name__ == "__main__"` set like native `python script.py args`, then tears the VM down (unless `--keep`).
- **Exit codes propagate**: an uncaught exception or `sys.exit(N)` in the script makes `colab run` exit non-zero (CPython semantics: `sys.exit()`/`sys.exit(0)` → 0, `sys.exit(N)` → N, `sys.exit("msg")` → 1).
- **Stream separation**: `colab run` writes its own `[colab] ...` chatter to **stderr** and the script's output to **stdout** — so `colab run job.py > out.txt` captures only the script's stdout. (`colab exec` streams the script's stdout/stderr live to your stdout/stderr.)
- Works as a shebang: `#!/usr/bin/env -S colab run --gpu T4` makes a `chmod +x`'d `.py` a self-contained "rent a GPU, run, clean up" script. After editing CLI behavior, reinstall before testing shebangs — they resolve `colab` via `$PATH`, not the editable install.
- A nonexistent script path exits non-zero **before** allocating a VM (no wasted compute).

### Automate
- `colab auth -s <name>` — VM-side GCP creds, needed before in-VM GCS/BigQuery calls (interactive; not agent-runnable).
- `colab drivemount -s <name> [PATH]` — mounts Drive at `/content/drive` by default (interactive; not agent-runnable).
- `colab install -s <name> pkg1 pkg2` — installs via `uv pip install --system`, falling back to `pip`. Also `colab install -s <name> -r requirements.txt`.

### Inspect & report
- `colab help` (or `colab help <cmd>`) lists/explains commands; the listing is alphabetical.
- `colab sessions` lists server-side assignments and auto-prunes stale local entries. Orphans with no local record show as `[?]`.
- `colab status [-s <name>]` shows hardware, IDLE/BUSY, and last execution.
- `colab log -s <name> [-n 20] [-t TYPE]` shows recent structured events; invaluable when a task fails.
- `colab log -s <name> -o summary.ipynb` exports the session as a notebook (also `.md`, `.txt`, `.jsonl` by suffix).
- `colab url -s <name>` prints a browser URL that attaches the Colab web UI to your existing CLI session instead of allocating a new VM (add `--open` to launch it).
- `colab skill` / `colab readme` print this skill and the README (handy for self-discovery).

## Safety
- **Always `colab stop -s <name>` when done** — idle VMs burn compute units. `colab run` (without `--keep`) self-cleans even if the script errors.
- Local state lives in `~/.config/colab-cli/sessions.json` (settings in `settings.json`, history in `history/*.jsonl`). Don't edit by hand.
- **Isolate parallel/agent runs** with the global `--config <path>` flag to point session state at a scratch file (e.g. `colab --config /tmp/agent.json new -s job`).

## Recovery
- "Session not found" / 404 / 401 on exec: the backend pruned the VM. `colab exec`/`repl` detect this and clean up local state automatically — run `colab sessions` and re-create with `colab new`.
- Execution timeout or wedged kernel: `colab restart-kernel -s <name>` (keeps the VM, resets the kernel), or `colab stop` then `colab new`.

---
name: colab-gamekit
description: Agent-directed optional Colab compute, one-shot testing and normal cleanup without a gateway or watchdog.
---
Read references/compute-kit.md and the official mirrored colab-operator SKILL.md. User chose direct Agent scheduling; never deploy a gateway, Cloudflare runtime, independent watchdog or background lease service for compute. Use available authenticated CLI/MCP only, with explicit budget and real lifecycle capabilities. Do not store OAuth credentials in source, KV, prompts or logs. Check installed CLI version and help, read-only sessions. Prepare scripts and dependencies before allocation. Prefer official colab run -s UNIQUE_NAME [--gpu T4] SCRIPT.py without --keep; verify actual CLI flags and accelerator allowlist, account quota and rate. CPU may suffice; CUDA does not prove graphics. Use MCP only if actual create/execute/result/delete-runtime/list tools exist and authorization permits. If explicit session handling needed, do it entirely in one uninterrupted invocation, with try/finally stop and verification. Never leave a runtime open across model reasoning, tool turns or user wait; default release after batch. Record owned runtime identity and cleanup result. Uncertain creation/cleanup blocks further paid jobs for that agent until reconciled; manual Colab session management is the fallback. No cross-agent atomic budget guarantee; each agent separately authorized and budgeted. No live runtime tested in release.
